recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs have sufficient material and staff resources to adequately perform their tasks, in accordance with Article 5(2)(b)(i) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Both CBs doubled the number of operators under their control in recent years. This huge increase was not accompanied by a proportionate readjustment in their resources, including staff, to carry out control and certification tasks. The ratio of inspections per inspector/year is very high, especially in certain periods in the year. The majority of operators in Bulgaria are plant producers, which narrows the timeframe to execute the inspections. As a result, a significant percentage of inspections are not carried out at the most suitable time, which renders these controls ineffective. This is not in line with Article 5(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted several cases, including all the inspections witnessed at plant producers, when inspections had been planned after harvesting had already taken place and with no products in the 10 warehouses. In addition, CB1 does not necessarily plan visits to processors at the time when organic products are processed, with the exception of the first inspection for the approval of new operators. This is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, which establishes that the nature of controls shall be determined based on an assessment of the risk of occurrence of irregularities and infringements as regards compliance with the requirements laid down in the same Regulation.

CBs do not necessarily require the operators to submit important compulsory information, such as on the precautionary measures, or do not adequately asses it. In addition, the number of staff available for certification and control tasks is very limited. As a result, the timing and preparation of the annual and additional visits are not always adequate, which strongly undermines the effectiveness of controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that risk analysis carried out by CBs serve as a good basis to determine the intensity of the unannounced or announced annual inspections an visits, as required by Article 92(c)(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and in particular that: Criteria such as quantities produced and past records as regards compliance are taken into account for the risk assessment, as required by Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; All operators are subject to risk assessment All subcontracted activities are subject to the same level of controls, in line with Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

citations.text: CB2 does not carry out the same type of annual inspection to all operators. Subcontracted operators, which carry out important core activities such as production, are not subject to the same level of control from the CB as certified operators. The CB uses a different checklist and carries out only short inspections, with significant scope limitations, in comparison to those carried out on certified operators. The CB stated that they considered subcontracted operators less risky operators as they were under the internal control of the client to whom they sell their products. This is the approach followed by CBs when issuing certification to Producer Groups in developing countries, but in MSs this is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, as the nature of these controls is not justified by any assessment of the risk of occurrence of irregularities as regards compliance. This is also not in line with Article 92(c)(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, which establishes that the result of risk analysis shall provide the basis for determining the intensity of unannounced or announced annual inspections and visits. 11

Both CBs use risk analysis procedures to select the operators for additional visits and sampling. Several criteria are used, such as past irregularities, time in the control system, number and types of crops grown, multiple activities carried out, parallel production and processing of organic and conventional products. The criteria are put together in several groups, which may score a maximum of five points. The scoring of the different groups is aggregated, and according to the final score, operators are allocated into risk groups.

The audit team noted the following weaknesses in the risk analysis implemented by both CBs: Some operators such as small farmers who do not market, and small traders selling only pre-packed products, are not subject to risk assessment by CB2. This is not in line with Article 65(2) and 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, which establishes that the selection of the operators where samples have to be taken and the random control visits shall be based on the general evaluation of the risk of non-compliance with the organic production rules. Quantities produced are not taken into account, which is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EU) No 889/2008. Operators with major non-compliances in previous years may remain in lower risk categories as the maximum possible score for each group is five points, regardless of the severity and recurrence of the non-compliance. In addition, risk assessment is carried out by CB2 inspectors during the inspection and information obtained by other sources (e.g. results of samples taken during previous years) is not taken into account by the CB. This is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Several important criteria are put together in the same group and the individual weight of each criterion may not be taken sufficiently into account as the maximum possible score for the all the criteria together in the group is five points. Operators placed in the second lowest category by CB1 may be selected before operators placed in a higher risk category for additional visits or sampling.

At the time of the DG Health and Food Safety audit, less than 0.050% of operators under the control of CB1 and CB2 were classified in the highest risk category. The majority of operators were placed in the second lowest risk category by CB1 while CB2 only had two risk categories, meaning that more than 99,9% of operators were placed in the lowest risk category. The audit team observed a number of cases where operators with low risk profiles (e.g. small fully organic farmer with no past irregularities) were placed in the same risk category as operators with a high risk profile (e.g. large producer and processor of conventional and organic products with past irregularities). This means that the risk assessment carried out by both CBs is inadequate and does not allow for the determination of the nature and frequency of controls, which is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 12

Risk analysis as carried out by CBs does not serve as a good basis to determine the nature and frequency of the visits to operators. Compulsory requirements such as quantities or past records are not adequately taken into account, not all operators are subject to risk assessment and not all subcontracted activities subject to the same level of controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that operators notify to CBs all relevant information necessary for the adequate planning and preparation of the inspections, and in particular that The information referred to in Article 63(1) (a) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 is transmitted by operators before the first control arrangements are in place; That the CBs adequately verify it, in line with Article 63(2) of the same Regulatio

citations.text: The inadequate timing may also be caused by insufficient knowledge of the operators to be visited. CB1 does not request the operators to submit information on all of their undertakings, but only on the parcels or units subject to organic certification. Precautionary measures, which are important prerequisites to comply with the organic production rules, are not required to be submitted to the CB either. This is not in line with Article 63(1) (a) and (d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. As a result, the CB does not verify the description of the units and the precautionary measures. This is not in line with Article 63(2) of the same Regulation. CB1 had not noted that, for more than one year, one operator produced a particular variety of plant under both conventional and organic management, which is not permitted in EU Regulations. Most of inspectors from CB1 did not know basic aspects such as the risk category of the operators visited or the precautionary measures implemented by operators to reduce the risk of contamination.

CB2 receives from their operators the information referred to in Article 63(1) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. However, the audit team noted cases where it was not used adequately. As an example, the CB manager evaluated the information on the operator and signalled points of attention for the inspector to focus on during the inspection. The annual inspection was planned after both the organic and conventional plots had been harvested. This rendered the inspection ineffective. The inspector was requested to check that the organic operator had sold the harvest as conventional rather than focusing on the only risky point, which was the presence of a conventional neighbouring plot.

CBs do not necessarily require the operators to submit important compulsory information, such as on the precautionary measures, or do not adequately asses it. In addition, the number of staff available for certification and control tasks is very limited. As a result, the timing and preparation of the annual and additional visits are not always adequate, which strongly undermines the effectiveness of controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all CBs carry out additional visits: 32 Primarily unannounced, as required by Article 65(4) or Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, Of at least to 10% of the operators under contract in accordance with the risk category, as required by Article 92(c)(2)(b) of the same Regulation and that at least 10% of all inspections and visits carried out by CBs are unannounced, in accordance with Article 92(c)(2)(c) of the same Regulation, and that the selection of operators for unannounced visits is determined on the basis of the risk analysis carried out by CBs

citations.text: CB1 carries out the additional visits primarily unannounced, which is in line with EU Regulations. However, the number of additional visits does not reach the minimum 10% of the total number of operators, which is not in line with Article 92c(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The total number of unannounced visits is also not reached, which is not in line with Article 92c(2)(c) of the same Regulation. Moreover, the audit team noted that most of the additional inspections carried out by CB1 in 2014 were concentrated in November and December. This undermines the effectiveness of the inspections as no relevant activity was carried out at that time in plant producers. CB2 could not provide any evidence that it carries out any additional visits based on risk, which was considered by the audit team as being the absence of a key control. In fact, the procedure for risk assessment had been implemented for the first time in 2014 and actually carried out by inspectors, meaning that all visits were planned before the categorization of operators took place. The audit checked a number of files claimed by the CB as relating to additional controls and noted that they were carried out to operators with low risk profile and by following a shortest report template. Moreover, the audit team noted that in several cases the inspection had taken place on the same day as the annual inspection. In other cases it was carried out to supplement the annual inspection. Furthermore, operators may be given a prior warning of 24 hours. All of this is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Conclusions on Planning and Prioritisation of Controls

The number of additional visits and unannounced visits does not meet the minimum requirements in EU Regulations. The selection of operators for additional visits and sampling is not always carried out risk-based. Moreover, additional visits are not primarily carried out unannounced in all cases and annual visits are always announced, which is not in line with EU Regulations. 13 5.2.4 Controls of Operators Legal Requirements Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs follow standard control procedures as required by Article 27(6)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, to ensure consistency and effectiveness of controls, and in particular that the procedures include: The units for non-organic products, as required by Article 66(3) of Regulation No 889/2008; To check records showing the effectiveness of the cleaning measures in facilities where conventional products are also processed, in line with Article 26 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; To check records showing the results of verification at reception of organic products and the balance between inputs and outputs, as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

citations.text: Both CBs have documented procedures to carry out controls. The main document used for the inspections is the report template, which also serves as a checklist for the inspectors. A copy of the report is given to operators, including the description of non- compliances and deadlines for the operators to apply corrective measures, which are followed-up by inspectors during the following inspection. However, the checklists used by the CBs did not provide the basis for assurance on the following important aspects as they failed to cover: Records showing the effectiveness of cleaning measures in facilities where parallel processing of conventional and organic foodstuffs take place, as required by Article 26 (4)(b)of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Records showing the results of verifications made on reception of organic foodstuffs, as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Operators did not keep such records and did not provide any evidence that they systematically checked the origin of products. This lack of verification was the root cause of at least one case notified from other MSs (see paragraph 97). Accounting documents showing the balance between input/output, as required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. No reference to the obligation of inspectors to physically inspect all conventional units run by the operator, as required by Article 66(3) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

This lack of adequate documented procedures is also not in line with Article 27(6)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, which establishes that the standard control procedure of CBs must contain a detailed description of the control measures and precautions that the body undertakes to impose on operators subject to its control.

Both CBs have documented procedures in place with the aim of ensuring consistency of controls. However, the level of detail is not adequate to provide inspectors with adequate guidance. Checklists do not include the verification of records showing the effectiveness of cleaning, the results of verification at reception and the balance between input/output. Operators are not required to keep such records and consequently, most operators do not keep them, thus not providing evidence that the relevant requirements have been complied with. In addition, units where non-organic products are produced or kept are not necessarily subject to the minimum control requirements.

recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs adequately verify the documents and information provided by operators, in particular: The suitability of the 3 km area surrounding the siting of organic apiaries, to guarantee that nectar and pollen sources consist essentially of crops and spontaneous vegetation as described in Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; The minimum surface areas indoors and outdoors and other characteristics of housing as established in Article 10 (3) and (4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. 33

citations.text: When records and accounting documents were available at the operators, inspectors did not adequately check them and other relevant requirements were often overlooked: CB1 inspectors signed and stamped the internal records checked and made a 14 reference in the report and attached a copy of these records to the report. One inspector from CB1 stated that he always stamps and signs on the records. This could be considered as a good audit practice as the performance of the inspectors can be traced back and subject to later evaluation. However, this inspector had not checked the records on the use of fertilizers and PPPs during the previous inspection, as there were no stamps or signatures on any of these. Furthermore, the control does not include checks on the official logbook filled by the official agricultural services. CB2 inspectors never leave a track of the documents checked, neither by leaving a mark on them nor by making a cross-reference in the report. In a large processor, the inspector could not document how he had calculated during the most recent annual inspection at that processor, the balance input-output for all the products processed since the previous inspection. The inspector claimed that the input of 279 tonnes of fruits had been validated only one day before the annual inspection at the processor at the wild collection area, based on estimation of harvest. The audit team checked the delivery notes and noted that all of the quantities had been delivered by one single person. The CB and the operator explained that compliance with the organic production rules is ensured by employing 16 seasonal workers who are given training and instructions to pick up the wild fruit. However, the audit team noted that each picker had collected around 300-400 kilos/day, which is unrealistic. The operator stated that these figures were not plausible and that he was aware that in practice a significant number of other pickers help in the collection and concluded that this activity was entirely out of their control. This lack of adequate verification of quantities harvested in wild collection areas could be the cause of the increasing number of irregularities notified from other MSs affecting wild collected products (see paragraph 95). The same inspector stated that he systematically verifies the records of own- checks carried out by the operator, even if no track of this verification is included in the report. However, the audit team noted that several samples taken by the operator and tested by accredited laboratories in July 2015 showed the presence of several unauthorised PPPs. The operator did not notify the positive results to the CB and the CB overlooked these results during the annual inspection carried out in September 2015. As a result, no measures were taken by the operator or by the CB to prevent the suspicious products from being marketed. This is not in line with Articles 91(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. No notification was made to the CU on the likelihood of non-compliance, which is not in line with Article 5(2)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Both CBs validate the quantities harvested by comparing the production declared with the estimations made by the operators. However, it remained unclear how plausibility checks, such as verification of the yield, were carried out by CBs. CBs do not use official yield data available on the website of the Ministry. The 15 data refers to conventional crops in the different regions of the country, and the CA accepts a variation of 20% in the yield when it comes to crops produced organically. In addition, only a small number of invoices for sales are usually checked, which is not representative of the total production/processing of the year. This is not in line with Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. In a small beekeeper, the CB2 inspector did not provide evidence that he had cross-checked the information on the map provided by the beekeeper during the annu

When such records or, any other document, such as maps showing the areas surrounding beehives are present, they are not adequately verified by inspectors to ensure compliance of operators with EU requirements. In addition, inspectors do not notice gross non- compliances regarding relevant requirements such as prohibited dehorning practices, inadequate husbandry and animal welfare conditions, proving such inspections to be ineffective. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 23(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Regulation. Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Article 27(13) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 17 Findings Controls carried out by the CA.

recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs adequately carry out labelling and traceability checks, and in particular that CBs verify that: Final products bear only the labels approved by CBs according to their procedures, and that labels are compliant with Article 23 or Regulation (EC) No 83472007. Identity checks are carried out by operators, as required by Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; Organic products are clearly identifiable at all times while stored in the operators´ facilities, as required by Article 35 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and that operators are able to trace the products throughout all production stages, to guarantee the balance between inputs and outputs, as required by Article 66(2) of the same Regulatio

citations.text: CBs approved in advance the labels used by operators. CBs receive and assess the format of the labels, which can only be used after the CB notify the operators. However, the audit team noted that in some cases, the labels used were not fully in line with the EU Regulations (e. g. blue logo used on a white background or letters difficult to read due to a transparent background). In two cases, products not satisfying the requirements of the EU Regulations bore labels including the term "bio" in the trademarks, which is not in line with Article 23(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

CBs carry out labelling and traceability checks during inspections at operators. Checklists used by CBs contain a specific aide-memoir for labelling and traceability checks to be performed at operators. However, the audit team noted that checks were not always adequate: Inspectors did not request or did not adequately verify records on the identity checks to be performed by operators. This is not in line with Article 66 of Regulation (EC) 889/2008 which establishes that operators shall keep documentary records proving that they have performed identity checks on the purchased products to verify that the labels or invoices contain the information referred to in Article 33 of Regulation (EC) 889/2008. In several cases, operators did not keep records showing the results of verification of the raw materials purchased. Inspectors did not require the operators to keep identified at all times stored products, as required by Article 35 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Neither did they require the operators to establish the links between different stages of processing, and therefore the balance between inputs and outputs could not always be fully validated for certain batches. This is not in line with Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

Labelling and traceability controls are regularly performed by the CA and CBs. Controls carried out by the CA are overall adequate. However, controls by CBs are not always exhaustive. Inspectors do not either require the operators to keep records on the identity checks carried out or to keep the products identified at all times allowing for establishing the link between the processing steps. Nevertheless, the outcome of the traceability exercise carried out during the audit was satisfactory for the products selected. As regards labelling checks, CBs do not systematically verify that the approved labels are used on the final products and it cannot be ensured that labelling of the products complies with EU provisions. 5.2.6 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 65 (2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Articles 5(2) and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that all CBs take and analyse samples for the purposes and under the conditions indicated in Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and in particular that A minimum number of samples corresponding to at least 5% the number of operators under its control are taken annually; Operators are selected on the basis of the general evaluation of the risk of non-compliance with the organic production rules.

citations.text: The selection of the operators by CB2 was not risk-based because there are only two operators in the highest risk category and the operators in the lower risk categories are randomly selected. The audit team noted several cases where samples were taken from operators with a low risk profile. In addition, around 60% of samples in 2014 and 40% in 2015 were taken from the same product, which is not representative of the activities controlled by the CB. This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008, which establishes that the selection of operators for sampling shall be based on the general evaluation of the risk of non-compliance with organic rules.

The audit team noted that in several cases, CB2 took a good number of samples at one processor on the same day and counted them as having been taken from the suppliers of the raw materials concerned. As a result of this practice, the total number of samples was artificially increased by 50% in 2014 and 2015. Without this practice, the CB did not reach the minimum number of samples required. In addition, six out of 11 CBs reported to the CA that they had taken during 2014 a number of samples which did not reach the minimum required, with two CBs not taking any sample at all. This is not in 20 line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2004, which establishes that the number of samples to be taken and analysed by CBs every year shall correspond to at least 5 % of the number of operators under its control. The insufficient number of controls (in the case of two CBs the absence of controls) raise concerns, as such controls are required in order to mitigate significant risks.
Not all CBs reach the minimum number of samples to be taken for the analysis of substances not authorised in organic production.

It cannot be ensured that the selection of the operators to be sampled is risk-based, that the quantities sent to the laboratories are sufficient and that samples are preserved, at least in the case of perishable products for the detection of PPPs. These deficiencies undermine the reliability of results. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. recommendations.text: Ensure that sampling procedures are adequate to guarantee the representativeness and preservation of the samples, and that CBs adequately follow them, in particular that: Samples taken from perishable products are preserved, in line with Section 4.6 of the Annex of Directive 2002/63/EC; Samples are transmitted to laboratories in quantities indicated in the CBs´ procedures;

citations.text: Both CBs have sampling instructions to serve as guidance to inspectors on how samples should be collected and transported to laboratories. Instructions by CB2 refer to the fulfilment of the requirements of Directive 2002/63/EC, which establishes the methodology to be followed for the testing of PPPs, including quantities to be sent to the laboratory for each type of product and conditions for the preservation of samples. However, the audit team checked several files and noted that the CB often did not follow its own procedure. Samples were sent to laboratories in quantities smaller than indicated in the Directive. In addition, samples were not preserved, which is not in line with Section 4.6 of the Annex of the Directive 2002/63/EC. This can render these checks ineffective.

Instructions issued by CB1 specify the equipment to be used and also the techniques to ensure the representativeness of the sample. The instructions do not require that the samples of perishable products are kept cool when delivered to the laboratories, which is not in line with Section 4.6 of the Annex of Directive 2002/63/EC. The audit team observed the procedure for taking samples followed by CB1. The inspector stated that a cooling box is used to transport the samples to the headquarters of the CB. However, the sample had to be sent to a laboratory in another MS and the CB does not use specific containers to preserve the sample cooled. In addition, the inspector used a plastic jar provided by the farmer to take the sample of the product, not following the CB´s sampling procedure.

It cannot be ensured that the selection of the operators to be sampled is risk-based, that the quantities sent to the laboratories are sufficient and that samples are preserved, at least in the case of perishable products for the detection of PPPs. These deficiencies undermine the reliability of results. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. recommendations.text: Ensure that laboratories entrusted with the analysis of PPPs residues in organic products are designated as required by Article 12(1) and (2) of 34 Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and their designation communicated to the National Reference Laboratory to facilitate the activities specified in Article 33(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Laboratories are not designated by the CU in advance and during the supervision of CBs, the CU does not check that laboratories have the appropriate scope to carry out the tests requested by CBs. The CU argued that the only requirement established in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 is that laboratories used by CBs operate in accordance with the standards referred to in Article 12(2) of the same Regulation (ISO 17025). However, the same Article also establishes that these laboratories may only be designated by the CU if they operate and are assessed and accredited to that standard. In addition, Article 12(3) establishes that such accreditation and assessment may relate to individual tests or groups of tests, which is not cross-checked by the CU.

As the CU does not designate the laboratories analysing official samples, it does not notify them to the National Reference Laboratory, thus not ensuring that the laboratories take part in the proficiency tests organised at national level, as indicated in Article 33(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

CBs have sampling programmes in place for the detection of substances not authorised in organic production. Action is taken by CBs in all cases where analytical results show any presence of unauthorised substance. Laboratories used are accredited to ISO 17025. However, laboratories are not designated by the CU, who does not check during supervision whether the analytical scope of the laboratories used by CBs is adequate. In addition, it is not ensured that laboratories carrying out official controls take part on the proficiency tests organised by the National Reference laboratory.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the description of tasks delegated to CBs as referred to in Article 5(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 includes the body responsible to decide on the range of PPPs to be requested for testing, and that CBs checks that the scope of accreditation of the laboratories used is adequate for all individual tests or groups of tests carried out, as established in Article 12(3) of the same Regulatio

citations.text: CB1 only requests the laboratories to use multi-residues methods. This is not adequate as some PPPs commonly used in the EU (for example Glyphosate and Chlormequat) can 21 only be detected by using methods that are specific for the relevant PPP. The sample sheet used by CB2 caters for other PPPs but Glyphosate is not included either. The delegation of tasks to CBs does not describe who is responsible to decide on the range of PPPs to be tested, taking into account relevant information available. This is not in line with Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Both CBs use laboratories accredited to ISO Guide 17025, which establishes the general requirements for the sampling and calibrating laboratories. The audit team checked several laboratory results and noted that the scope of the laboratories was adequate for the methods used and substances tested. However, CB2 does not systematically check that the scope of the chosen laboratory is appropriate. The audit team noted that CB2 kept an old version of the accreditation certificate of the laboratory often used by the CB. citations.text: According to the National Regulation, the CU has the competence to grant derogations, except derogations on the use of conventional seeds and propagating material, which had been delegated to CBs, in line with EU Regulations. The National Regulation also includes provisions for certain derogations which, although not granted in recent years, are not in line with, or already phased out in EU Regulations. For example, CBs may grant derogations for the renewal of herds and flocks and for the introduction of non- organic female mammals, which is not in line with Article 42 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The National Regulation also foresees the possibility to grant derogations on housing conditions and stocking densities, already phased out in EU Regulations since 31 December 2013.

All derogations granted by CBs concerned the use of conventional seeds. When examining applications submitted, CBs must check whether operators justify the use of the conventional seed and also prove that no organic seed was available at that time in the market. At the time of the DG Health and Food Safety audit, there were eight organic suppliers registered in the seed database to supply organic seed and other 23 propagating material (see paragraph 105). The audit team noted that in several cases, operators had used a conventional seed without applying for a derogation, contrary to Article 45(6) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The audit team also noted that some derogations were granted in 2014 by CBs without operators providing any evidence that the same variety of the organic seed was not available. The CU and the CBs stated that the seed database was not operative at that time. However, operators did not either provide any evidence that there were no suppliers able to deliver the organic seed, which is not in line with Article 45(5)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

The National Regulation establishes the derogations and exceptions to organic rules to be granted by the CU and CBs. It also includes provisions for certain derogations which, although not granted in recent years, are not in line with, or already phased out in EU Regulations.

The CU correctly grant derogations for the applications received. However, it cannot be ensured that operators use conventional seeds only after a derogation is granted by CBs. Moreover, CBs often do not request operators to prove the unavailability in the market of the same organic variety.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the measures implemented in cases of infringements are effective, dissuasive and proportionate, as required by Article 55(1) of 35 Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The CU has adopted and notified to CBs a catalogue of enforcement measures to be applied in cases of non-compliances, in line with Article 92(d) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, although its adoption was late3. The measures are contained in Annex III to the National Regulation.4 The measures range from a simple remark or warning to total withdrawal of the operators from the system, depending on the severity of the non- compliance. However, most of the measures foreseen are not adequate to ensure compliance of operators with organic requirements. For the following non-compliances, operators will only receive warnings with no suspension of the certification, even if no corrective action is taken: Parallel conventional and organic production of the same variety of plant or of the same animal species, if conventional and organic productions were kept separately; No records at all are kept by plant producers during two consecutive years; Use of conventional seeds without prior authorisation when the same variety was available in organic form; Use of large quantities of unauthorised conventional feed; Dehorning of animals during three consecutive years without prior authorisation by the CU and without anaesthesia; Non respect of conversion period for animals exceeding the maximum number of treatments by chemically synthesised allopathic medicines; Severe infringement regarding outdoor space and housing conditions; Use of non-organic ingredients other than those authorised in Annex IX to Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 even if the same organic ingredient was available. 3 The catalogue became effective only in August 2014 as compared to the EU Requirement (1 January 2014). 4 In their response to the draft report, the CA noted that " The CU has initiated a procedure to amend the Regulation, and more specifically the catalogue of sanctions imposed for the different types of infringements." 26

The sanction catalogue does not adequately take into account the repetition of non- compliances, and for some of them (for example dehorning without prior authorisation) operators may receive a "remark" the first year, a "corrective instruction" the second and a "warning" the third. After 24 months with no repetition of the irregularity, past records are disregarded. No monetary sanctions are foreseen, even in cases where no corrective action may be taken (for example when non-compliant product has already been sold as organic and it cannot be recalled from the market).This is not in line with Article 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, which establishes that measures must be proportionate and dissuasive.

CBs follow the national sanction catalogue. For the non-compliances noted by the audit team during the visits at operators (see bullet points in paragraph 48) CB1 only reported remarks to the operators concerned and the certification was granted in all cases with no need of corrective measures to be applied by the operators. The CB stated that the non- compliance would be followed-up during the annual inspection in 2016.

One of the few measures found to have consequences for the operators´ certification were those applied by CB1 concerning the use of unauthorised PPPs (see paragraph 71). However, the sanction catalogue only foresees the prohibition of operators from marketing any organic products for short periods (up to 12 months) if they are found to use unauthorised substances during several consecutive years.

The CU has adopted and notified to CBs a catalogue of infringements and corresponding measures to be applied by CBs. However, most of the measures applied are neither dissuasive nor proportionate, and therefore ineffective to ensure compliance of the 28 operators with organic requirements.

Findings

The laboratories visited could provide the results for all the samples delivered to them and these were evaluated by the FVO audit team. For the reasons mentioned below, the results were not credible. Only one laboratory provided credible results. While this had been identified in a number of laboratories, only one (NRL) had documented these anomalies. However, no follow-up action had been taken by the official services and official controls had not detected problems with the lack of credibility of analysis results.

The results of the tests carried out in different public or private laboratories differed very significantly, with some public laboratories identifying high or very high numbers of unsatisfactory results, while the private laboratories identified hardly any non- compliance even when performing a high number of analyses including in the same geographical areas. The range went from zero to 30% for TPC and SCC.

In a high proportion of cases raw milk samples taken by an official or the FBO at holding level had been manipulated. They had been diluted before being submitted for analysis: this was evident when the values for fat content and/or freezing point were taken into consideration. For example, many examples were seen where the fat content was lower than 1%. This was also the case for official samples taken in the framework of the process for the classification of holdings. As a consequence the results for TPC and SCC were deemed satisfactory whereas, in reality, they would have been unsatisfactory if they had not been diluted prior to analysis.

When subjected to statistical analysis, it was found that the results of samples collected by specific FBOs on different holdings were lower than or approaching the limits of repeatability of the methods (for example 6,6 % at a level 140 000 cells where the acceptable variation limit was 10 % when analysing the same samples twice). Usually, results showing 50% to 90% (depending of the level of TPC or SCC) of variation are expected with such microbiological reference methods. This was the case for one laboratory, in particular, where a high number of analyses had been carried out. In such cases, it cannot be excluded that the sampling supposed to come from different holdings came from one single holding or that "standardised" samples had been prepared for submission for laboratory analysis. This suspicion is reinforced by implausible interval between collection of samples from different holdings (see paragraph 32 above).

Samples submitted for laboratory analysis for SCC and TPC showed evidence of having been manipulated in order to obtain satisfactory results. recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authority puts in place a system to verify the effectiveness of official controls performed in relation to the import of live animals, products of animal and non-animal origin as required by Article 4(2)(a), Article 4(6) and Article 8(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Whilst information and instructions are provided to the BIP and DPEs/DPI staff to support the implementation of the import controls the lack of sufficiently detailed guidance has resulted in situations where the official controls were not performed correctly and having a consistent approach. In addition, the national administrative provisions on animal health requirements for the importation of live animal species which are not regulated by EU legislation have not been established, therefore there is a possibility that such consignments would be accepted for importation without due consideration of the risks they may pose. 5

The audit team checked in total 11 files related to import of live animals and noted the following errors in documentation which did not elicit an appropriate response from the authorities: A consignment of birds (one parrot imported for non-commercial use) had been imported with an appropriate model veterinary certificate, but the applicable parts of the health certificate had not been filled in, contrary to the requirements of Annex II to Commission Decision 2007/25/EC. In one BIP, a consignment of horses had been imported with an appropriate model veterinary certificate (for re-entry) but some applicable parts of the health certificate (owner declaration) had not been filled in, as required by Annex II of Commission Decision 93/195/EEC. 6 In another BIP, several consignments of horses had been imported with an appropriate model veterinary certificate (for temporary admission) but some applicable parts of the health certificate (owner declaration) had not been filled in, as required by Annex II(E) of Commission Decision 92/260/EEC. 5.2.2 DOCUMENTARY CHECKS ON PRODUCTS OF ANIMAL ORIGIN

In one BIP, the competent authority considered that the time limit of 60 days applicable to rejected consignments, with a view to their re-dispatch, started from the moment of arrival of the consignment in the port. This interpretation is not in line with Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In the majority of the cases reviewed by the audit team during the BIP visits, consignments of food of animal origin were accompanied by prerequisite documents. In other cases the audit team identified a number of non-compliances in accompanying documents: In one BIP several consignments of wild fish were accepted for importation despite the fact that the health attestation referring to farmed stock was not crossed out. The competent authority stated that the health certificate was 7 checked against the catch certificate. The latter was not available for examination by the audit team. A consignment of casings was accepted for importation despite the fact that the non-applicable parts in the health attestation were not crossed out. 5.2.3 DOCUMENTARY CHECKS ON PRODUCTS OF NON-ANIMAL ORIGIN Findings
The competent authority incorrectly allowed the importation of a consignment of groundnuts from Argentina since the analytical report was issued after the signature of the health certificate.

In one DPE, several rejected consignments of groundnuts from different non-EU countries were not re-dispatched within the time limit of 60 days of the decision of the competent authority. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team noted that in these cases the re-dispatch took place up to three months after the signature of part II of the CED. Conclusion on the implementation of documentary checks

For the most part, the implementation of documentary checks is carried out correctly in BIPs and DPEs and performed using all available information. Nevertheless the audit team's identification of errors in documentation accompanying consignments which were ultimately imported, indicate that improvements are required in the implementation of documentary checks and subsequent decisions on importation.

The audit team noted a number of errors in the documentation in TRACES as follows: Two consignments of different products (farmed fish and animal by-products) were incorrectly declared by the person responsible for the load as transhipments in box 17 of part I of the CVED instead of definitive imports. The competent authority did not take any action to rectify these deficiencies during the documentary check. The competent authority correctly rejected a consignment of farmed fish due to a failure in the identity check, but the results of the identity check were recorded incorrectly as satisfactory in box 27 of part II of the CVED. There was no information in box 41 of part II of the CVED for confirmation of receipt from the local veterinary unit for two reimported consignments. However, the audit team noted that the BIP received a letter from the local veterinary units of destination confirming receipt of the consignments. For one rejected consignment of collagen for human consumption, the date of re- export was not recorded in box 35 of part II of the CVED as is required in the Notes 9 for guidance for the CVED certificate in Annex III to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. One consignment of wild fish had been incorrectly declared by the person responsible for the load as farmed stock in box 12 of part I of the CVED instead of wild fish as described in health certificate. This had not been spotted by the competent authority during the documentary check. Conclusion on the use of TRACES
The audit team noted that no audits or supervision activity had been carried out by the central level in BIPs/DPEs from 2015 until the time of this audit.

The audit team noted that no supervision activity had been performed at the local level with the exception of BIP Sofia airport where a regular supervision activity has been carried out at the local level since 2014. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 4(2)(a) and 4(4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on the verification of compliance of import controls

Lack of verification activities undermines the capacity of the central competent authority to ensure that official controls are performed correctly. Thus the competent 10 authority has not used relevant mechanisms to ensure that the official controls are appropriate and effective.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the relevant documented procedures are in place and available to the staff performing official controls as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: In line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the BCD has established procedures, guidance and instructions for implementing import controls. The instructions prepared by the BCD do not include sufficiently detailed information to support the work of the officials responsible for conducting documentary checks and to ensure a consistent approach in relation to: - actions to be taken in the event of non-compliances related to documentary checks being identified. The audit team noted that several errors in records it selected at random for examination had been accepted by the officials (see finding 31); - implementation of the time limits applicable for rejected consignments with a view to their re-dispatch (see findings 24 and 29). c. Since 2014, the BCD has developed procedures and working instructions for controls on food of non-animal origin. These were updated in 2017.

This interpretation is not in line with Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In other cases the audit team identified a number of non-compliances in accompanying documents: In one BIP several consignments of wild fish were accepted for importation despite the fact that the health attestation referring to farmed stock was not crossed out. The competent authority stated that the health certificate was 7 checked against the catch certificate. The latter was not available for examination by the audit team. A consignment of casings was accepted for importation despite the fact that the non-applicable parts in the health attestation were not crossed out. 5.2.3 DOCUMENTARY CHECKS ON PRODUCTS OF NON-ANIMAL ORIGIN Findings

For the most part, the implementation of documentary checks is carried out correctly in BIPs and DPEs and performed using all available information. Nevertheless the audit team's identification of errors in documentation accompanying consignments which were ultimately imported, indicate that improvements are required in the implementation of documentary checks and subsequent decisions on importation.

When non-compliances are identified during documentary checks the decision on further action is taken by the official and depending on the case, after internal consultation. However, the instructions provided by the BCD did not provide enough detailed information to the officials to support their decision contrary to Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions on the action taken in case of non-compliances related to documentary checks

When the DPE and BIP officials identify non-compliances during the documentary check, they take action, although not always the appropriate action. The lack of sufficiently detailed instructions from the competent authority hampers correct decision- making.

responses.response: Not later than end of March 2018, a special Order to be signed by the BFSA ED is to establish and set up a working group designated to update the current standard operating procedures for official controls and to develop detailed guidance for carrying out documentary checks, together with relevant actions to be performed in case of deficiencies identified.

citations.text: There were significant variations between regions in the implementation of the programme. recommendations.text: To improve implementation of active surveillance in domestic pigs and wild boars by underperforming counties in order to achieve targets set out in the EU co-financed veterinary programmes approved by the Commission for 2015, 2016 and 2017. 21

citations.text: Based on the data provided by the competent authority, they surpassed the total target set for industrial and type A holdings where animals had to be clinically examined, but not all regions achieved the targets set for them. In 2015, authorised veterinarians had to inspect 100% and official veterinarians 10% of backyard farms; in 2016, the surveillance scheme changed to 10% and 5% respectively.

Although with regional variations, the active surveillance programme for domestic pigs provides substantial guarantees that the CSF virus is not circulating in commercial holdings. The system gives more limited guarantees for holdings with low biosecurity, where shortcomings in holding registration and records undermine the ability to fully assess the CSF epidemiological situation but the sharp drop in the number of backyard holdings following comprehensive verification by the competent authority mitigates the significance of this weakness.

The team noted the following: The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars have been issued and implemented. In 2016, 49 wild boars were tested seropositive: all seropositive animals were tested negative by PCR. Age and location (oral vaccination in previous years) of each seropositive wild boar were compatible with the assumption that seropositivity was due to previous vaccination. However, no procedures are in place to confirm this assertion and discard other possible hypothesis (circulation of virus in the area). Therefore, appropriate measures to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease in wild boar when the disease is suspected, were not taken according to the requirements laid down in Article 15 of Directive 2001/89/EC (taking into account the recommendations of the CSF diagnostic manual: point B (3) and (7) of Chapter VII of Annex to Decision 2002/106/EC). The authorities issued new instructions regarding surveillance in wild boars in 2016 (No 6106 of 17 October 2016) requesting the sampling and testing (ASF and CSF) of all shot wild boars (ASF strategy to prevent or detect early the introduction of ASF in Bulgaria) and the request was renewed for the 2017 hunting season (letter dated 11 October 2017). These instructions have not been taken into account in two Regional Directorates visited during the audit. In addition, the 2016 and 2017 programmes have not been updated to take into consideration this new strategy, which would have led to a significant increase in testing expenses (about 90,000 wild boars were tested in 2016). The testing capacity of the laboratory has not been checked and assessed beforehand. The competent authority stated that the intention of these instructions was to raise the 14 awareness of hunters and develop the habit of systematic sampling, but that they had no intention to test all samples. In one region visited, the audit team noted under-implementation of the active surveillance programme in wild boars: e.g. respectively in 2015 and 2016, only 63 and 20 shot wild boars were sampled and tested, while the planned number of samples was 147. The region, where a vaccination programme was implemented until the end of 2015, was considered at risk, as it border a country with an unknown CSF status. The competent authority had an explanation for this situation, but no corrective action was initiated. The laboratories did not perform PCR testing for CSF since April 2017, due to a lack of test kits. According to the National reference laboratory, samples have been frozen pending further testing.

The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since the authorities issued guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars for the CSF surveillance programme in 2013. The programme, as implemented, has adequate sensitivity for confirming absence of CSF virus circulation in wild boars. The significant under-performances in some regions lead to uncertainty regarding the disease status of these zones, especially for peripheral regions, where a vaccination programme has been implemented until recently. There are no procedures in place to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease when a wild boar is tested seropositive.

recommendations.text: To enhance passive surveillance in domestic pigs in order to ensure that CSF is being continuously ruled out as a potential cause of pig illness or mortality in line with the main criteria described in Chapter III of Annex to Decision 2002/106/EC.

citations.text: The team noted that: According to the central authority, since 2015 to date, only two occurrences of suspicion of CSF in domestic pigs were subject to laboratory tests. CSF was ruled out after getting negative results from the National reference laboratory 10 following the criteria laid down in the EU diagnostic manual for CSF. However, differential diagnosis with ASF was not carried out. Conclusions on surveillance, controls on domestic pigs

Passive surveillance in domestic pigs remains very weak and, as such, does not provide a sufficient level of confidence that CSF is being continuously ruled out as a potential cause of pig illness or mortality. This results in uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of the CSF early detection system. Furthermore, differential diagnosis with ASF is not carried out in cases of suspicion of CSF in domestic pigs.

In addition, the 2016 and 2017 programmes have not been updated to take into consideration this new strategy, which would have led to a significant increase in testing expenses (about 90,000 wild boars were tested in 2016). The testing capacity of the laboratory has not been checked and assessed beforehand. The competent authority stated that the intention of these instructions was to raise the 14 awareness of hunters and develop the habit of systematic sampling, but that they had no intention to test all samples. In one region visited, the audit team noted under-implementation of the active surveillance programme in wild boars: e.g. respectively in 2015 and 2016, only 63 and 20 shot wild boars were sampled and tested, while the planned number of samples was 147. The region, where a vaccination programme was implemented until the end of 2015, was considered at risk, as it border a country with an unknown CSF status. The competent authority had an explanation for this situation, but no corrective action was initiated. The laboratories did not perform PCR testing for CSF since April 2017, due to a lack of test kits. According to the National reference laboratory, samples have been frozen pending further testing.

Regarding passive surveillance, the audit team noted the following: Instructions for sampling of wild boars were not correctly implemented in two Regional Directorates visited, as the authorities did not understand that samples of wild boars killed on the road have to be sent to the laboratory. Since April 2017, no PCR testing for CSF has been performed in the framework of passive surveillance because of the lack of availability of test kits. ASF differential diagnosis was not performed on samples forwarded to the laboratory, even when requested by the competent authority. 15 Conclusions on surveillance in wild boars

The active surveillance system for wild boars has significantly improved since the authorities issued guidelines on the targeted sampling of wild boars for the CSF surveillance programme in 2013. The programme, as implemented, has adequate sensitivity for confirming absence of CSF virus circulation in wild boars. The significant under-performances in some regions lead to uncertainty regarding the disease status of these zones, especially for peripheral regions, where a vaccination programme has been implemented until recently. There are no procedures in place to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease when a wild boar is tested seropositive.

During the visit of the national reference laboratory, the team noted that: The laboratory has no laboratory information management system system, and therefore it was rather difficult to find the requested documents. Moreover, the laboratory has no crisis management plan as it had been running under crisis mode for the past couple of years (lumpy skin disease, avian influenza outbreaks). At reception level, in the absence of specific instructions, certain requests for testing were deliberately modified or not taken into account: e.g. even when requested by the authorities, ASF testing was not performed; in 2016, following a request for differential diagnosis (CSF, ASF and foot-and-mouth disease) on a wild boar sample coming from a region neighbouring Turkey, only CSF testing was performed. Moreover, since April 2017, incoming samples from wild boars found dead were not registered at reception: the laboratory explained to the team that this was applied in order to avoid impact on the turn-around time, which could affect its accreditation. The laboratory had only two pieces of PCR testing equipment at the time of the audit, of which one was not operational; consequently, the testing capacity of the laboratory was clearly deficient. The laboratory informed the team that two additional PCR devices will be purchased by the end of 2017; so that ASF testing can be performed on a routine basis. The only certified test for CSF virus detection is PCR. From April 2017, the national reference laboratory has not performed any PCR test , due to a lack of availability of test kits. The laboratory explained to the team that this was due to issues related to public procurement. o An alternative method (ELISA antigen), for which the laboratory is no longer accredited, was used in the pre-slaughter surveillance of East Balkan pigs. The central authorities were orally informed. o Regarding wild boar, since April 2017, all samples have been frozen and they are kept in cold storage until the PCR test is available again. In 2017, serological ELISA testing has been performed according to the surveillance scheme. However, in 2016, an internal audit carried out on the implementation of the CSF programme clearly identified in one region that 17 serological ELISA testing was not performed because the reference laboratory had run out of kits. Virus isolation and virus neutralisation for CSF are no longer accredited tests, and the laboratory hasn't been in a position to perform a virus neutralisation test since 2014. Currently, there is no agreement with the EURL for support in confirmation of positive samples by virus isolation and virus neutralisation. Virus neutralisation was not performed on ELISA seropositive wild boars. Therefore, appropriate measures to confirm or rule out the presence of the disease in wild boar when the disease is suspected, were not taken in accordance with EU requirements.

The significant shortcomings in the CSF national reference laboratory and one regional laboratory visited - mainly due to shortage of resources and inadequate organisation ­ impact negatively on the capacity of the authorities to early detect CSF.

citations.text: Bulgaria sends live pigs to other Member States accompanied by the appropriate Intra- Union trade certificate, signed on the basis of the current surveillance scheme. No specific instruction had been issued when Decision 2013/764/EU was modified in 2016 to introduce this derogation, and no specific check-list was developed to verify compliance with the provisions of Article 2a of this Decision. Live pigs certified for trade did not meet the requirements of Decision 2013/764/EU, as: The holding was not subjected at least every four months to inspections by the competent authority. Live pigs were introduced into the holding during the 30-day period immediately prior to the date of dispatch. The sampling and testing of the pigs was not performed within one month prior to movement to the slaughterhouse; 19 The testing was performed as per the annual plan, allowing for detection of 20% prevalence, while the requirement is that the testing should be performed according to the standard laid down in point F.2 of Chapter IV of the Annex to Decision 2002/106/EC (10% seroprevalence with 95% confidence (5% for sows) in pigs in each sub-unit in the holding). citations.text: There has been no systematic vaccination of calves since 15 July 2016. The policy to vaccinate calves was amended at a meeting between the CCA and all RFSD's in December 2016 when the age limit was reduced from 6 to 4 months of age. However, apart from the minutes of the meeting no specific instruction was issued to RFSD's and at the time of this audit, no systematic vaccination of calves had commenced.

As there has been no systematic vaccination of calves since 15 July 2016, there is a serious risk of an ever increasing number of susceptible animals in Bulgaria which could become infected if/when virus circulates. This risk would be addressed if the instruction issued on 13 February to vaccinate all calves over 4 months of age with immediate effect and to continue this on a weekly basis is implemented.

recommendations.text: Ensure that staff performing plant health checks are qualified to do so, in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, in particular that they are aware of the official work instructions for performing such checks, that they have available, information on interceptions made by other Member States, and that newly recruited staff are technically competent.

citations.text: The audit team confirmed with inspectors met during the audit, that they had undergone training as described by the BFSA. However, the audit team noted that two inspectors at Sofia Airport, who had recently completed their induction training, did not carry out an effective inspection of basil (see section 5.4.4 below). All other staff met by the audit team appeared to be fully technically competent.

Two staff at Sofia Airport, responsible for performing import checks for plant health, are not technically competent and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, at least to perform plant health checks, which is not in line with Article 1 of Directive 98/22/EC, in particular Point 2 of the Annex to that Directive. 4

The BFSA stated that they have issued official work instructions (see section 5.1.3 below) to ensure that, if followed, controls are performed appropriately and in line with Directive 2000/29/EC. However, at least in the case of sampling (see section 5.1.3) and dealing with soil attached to imported produce (see section 5.1.6 below), staff were generally not aware of these work instructions. The lack of awareness of official work instructions means that staff are not necessarily able to ensure the proper application of the Directive, and cannot therefore be considered as qualified, which is not in line with Article 2(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

Whilst observing an inspection of cut basil (Ocimum sp.) from Israel, inspectors stated that they were unaware of any interceptions having been notified on this trade elsewhere in the EU. In fact, at the time of the audit, basil was the second most frequently 6 intercepted commodity from Israel which in turn was the non-EU country with the fourth highest number of interceptions for harmful organisms in the EU1. These inspectors did not have available information on interceptions made by other Member States. This is not in line with Point 1 of the Annex to Commission Directive 98/22/EC. 5.1.4 Planning of official controls

The audit team noted that, at least in the case of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, the work instructions on sampling are generally not applied in practice (see section 5.1.3 above). It was also noted by the audit team that RFSD inspectors operating at approved places of inspection were not aware of sampling instructions for fruits, vegetables and cut flowers. The senior official from the region concerned confirmed that she was aware of such instructions but considered them to be out of date and no longer relevant. The BFSA later confirmed that the instructions were current and should have been known by the RFSD.

Two newly recruited staff at Sofia Airport are not technically competent to carry out plant health checks, as a result, their checks cannot be considered as reliable. The same staff were unaware of interceptions made in other Member States. Furthermore, whilst staff are familiar with most official instructions, there are instructions on certain topics, which inspectors are generally unaware of. As a result, plant health checks are not always carried out in line with the BFSA's work instructions which, compromises the reliability of these checks. The system of internal audits has not been effective in identifying and addressing this.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the sampling methodology applied in practice for plant health checks provides for a sample size which is representative, in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, in order to reasonably conclude that the lot is not contaminated with harmful organisms, in line with Article 13(1) of the same Directive.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, if applied, the sampling rates in the work instructions would, according to ISPM 31, provide an appropriate probability of detecting harmful organisms in small and large lots of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, and plants intended for planting. However, for mid-sized lots, the sample size would, in many cases, provide a confidence level significantly below 80% of detecting even a 5% level of infestation and this reduced level of confidence was not justified based on risk. The work instructions on sampling do not therefore provide for a sample which is large enough to be considered as representative, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The audit team noted that the work instructions on sampling are not generally applied in practice in the case of fruit, vegetables and cut flowers. All inspectors met by the audit team, other than those at Sofia Airport who followed the work instructions on sampling, stated that they sample 200 individual fruit, vegetables or stems, selected at random from 10 boxes, which is not in line with the work instructions.

The audit team observed an inspection of citrus from Turkey and noted that: the lot consisted of 2 200 boxes, each weighing 10 kilograms; the BCD inspectors selected 10 boxes from five different pallets and inspected 20 fruit from each box; according to the work instructions, the sample size should have been 88 boxes. The sample size taken in this case was therefore lower than that provided in the work instructions, which already provides for too low a confidence level. The sample was not therefore representative of the lot, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The work instructions provide for sample sizes which, in some cases, are too small to be considered representative of the lot and the sample sizes applied in practice are sometimes even smaller. Therefore, the resulting checks are not reliable in determining the pest status of the lot.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all interceptions are notified in accordance with Commission Directive 94/3/EC, in particular, interceptions made of plants, plant products and other objects imported in consignments considered as 'non-commercial' by the Single Authority, as required by Article 2 of the same Directive.

citations.text: At Sofia Airport, BCD inspectors stated that they work daily with the Customs Services in the passenger channels. Customs officers identify passengers for inspection and in the event that they are carrying any quantity of plant material, BCD inspectors are engaged to determine whether the material is compliant with import requirements. BCD inspectors stated that, at the time of the audit, two seizures had resulted from these passenger baggage controls so far in 2017, in both cases the quantities detected were in excess of the small quantity concession and no accompanying phytosanitary certificate was present. The BCD inspectors stated that they do not notify such interceptions through the EUROPHYT system because they are 'non-commercial' consignments. The BFSA stated that they considered 'non-commercial' consignments to include those sent by postal or courier modes and goods contained in travellers' personal baggage. The BFSA confirmed that the national policy was only to notify interceptions of 'commercial' consignments (see section 5.6 below). 5.3.6 Checks for non-regulated articles and for non-regulated harmful organisms

The audit team studied notifications submitted by Bulgaria and noted the notification procedures laid down in Commission Directive 94/3/EC are generally complied with. However, the BFSA do not notify interceptions related to passenger baggage (see section 5.3.5 above). Failure to notify these interceptions is not in line with the requirements of Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC.

Interceptions of 'non-commercial' consignments, in particular those imported in passengers' luggage, are not notified to the Commission and other Member States. This does not enable the Commission and other Member States to evaluate and potentially mitigate the risk posed by such imports.

citations.text: Laboratory procedures were available on-the-spot and generally followed the relevant international standards. However, some shortcomings were noted by the audit team: MIC determination Quality controls with reference strains were not run every day that the tests were performed in order to monitor the quality of test results, as detailed in ISO 20776:2006 and CLSI M07-A10. Instead, the reference strain was only run for 9 specific situations such as for the verification of new batches of testing microdilution plates or broth and for the performance of proficiency tests. There were no procedures in place to ensure that implausible test results are adequately challenged and investigated before being reported to EFSA. For instance, some isolates were reported showing resistance to cephalosporins and susceptibility to ampicillin, high values of resistance to nalidixic acid and susceptibility to ciprofloxacin. Whilst improvements have been noted in the quality of data reported since the inception of the programme in 2014, there are still no documented procedures or good practices to ensure a harmonised approach during plates reading. The MIC determination procedure for Campylobacter only included the incubation time/temperature conditions of 37ºC, 48 hours although the combination 42ºC, 24 hours was also used. Therefore, the standard operating procedures were not being followed. Although manual records were kept of the working temperature for each incubator (verification twice a day to check functioning), records were neither kept of the duration of incubation nor of the identification of the incubator used to allow for correlation between the results obtained and the incubation conditions. Moreover, relevant information such as the Muller-Hinton media used for the performance of the tests was not recorded. This insufficient record keeping is not in line with point 4.13.2 of ISO 17025. There was no calibration of the multichannel pipettes used to add the inoculum to the plate wells in order to ascertain the volume used which is not in line with point 5.4.1 of ISO 17025. Moreover, no alternative methods to obtain this information (for instance, through periodic control of the weight of the filled microdilution plates) were developed. Protocols for detection of presumptive E. coli producing ESBL and AmpC enzymes Reference strains are regularly used to validate the preparation of the McConkey agar with cefotaxime. Although these plates are usually prepared for a relatively short period (2 weeks), this shelf life had neither been defined in the internal procedures nor had the validation of the medium stability for this period ever been performed. For the year 2015, despite the fact that there were 92 presumptive ESBL-, AmpC- producing E. coli isolates gathered from the caecal samples, only 72 isolates were tested later on for the MIC determination. No investigation had been performed on this unusual recovery rate. 10 5.2.2.4 Storage of the isolates
