recommendations.text: Legal requirements Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires, inter alia, that "audits ........shall be carried out in a transparent manner". Section 5.2 of the Annex of Commission decision 2006/677/EC provides guidance on transparency, including the following: "In order to demonstrate the audit process is transparent, documented procedures should, in particular, include a clearly defined audit planning process, audit criteria and audit report approval and distribution mechanisms. Management and implementation of the audit process should be transparent to all relevant stakeholders. In particular, there should be full transparency between the audit body and the auditee. Ensuring the audit process is transparent in the eyes of other stakeholders will assist in the dissemination of information, and in particular in the sharing of best practice within and between competent authorities. The Member States should adopt the appropriate measures to ensure their audit systems are transparent, taking national legal and other requirements into account. To that end, the Member States should consider encouraging practices that improve the transparency of the process."

Findings 102. The Audit Unit ensures transparency towards its auditees by communicating the audit plan, process and objectives to the auditee before conducting the audit, allowing the auditee to make comments on the draft report before it is finalised, and distributing the audit report to both the regional and central level directors concerned. 103. The BFSA publishes on its website its multi-annual audit programme, its risk methodology, its audit procedure including annexes, and its annual reporting on audit activities in the context of the annual report on the implementation of the MANCP. Conclusions on transparency 104. There are appropriate, clearly documented arrangements in place to ensure auditees have a clear understanding of the audit process and its outputs. 105. The publication of information on audit activities provides assurance to relevant external stakeholders about the role of the audit function in improving the quality of official controls. 28 5.3 Challenges reported by the competent authority 106. The Audit Unit described the challenges it faces as follows: a. There are certain difficulties in providing the appropriate auditors and/or relevant technical experts needed to perform the necessary expert assessment of official controls along the whole food chain. Maintaining and enhancing the knowledge and qualifications of auditors by conducting specialised training so that they have the necessary expertise and competence to carry out audits of official controls is also challenging. b. There is also a need to ensure that the requirements for independent review of the audit process are better met, so that the audit process can better fulfil its objectives. c. Conducting audits with a stronger focus on the effectiveness of official controls. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The MAFF has put audit arrangements in place which serve as an external review of the implementation of the official controls carried out by the BFSA. In response to information received after the audit, it can be concluded that the MAFF has also put in place internal audit arrangements for its own official control activities vis-à-vis the central level tasks and supervision it performs in relation to Control Bodies. With regard to the audit arrangements of the BFSA, there is a robust and sufficiently transparent internal audit system in place. Independent scrutiny of the audit process has been carried out and has provided external assurances about the arrangements in place. The Audit Unit comprises a team of well-qualified, competent and experienced auditors, who are able to deliver comprehensive system audits of high quality. They are supported by a pool of auditors and technical experts who help deliver an extensive programme of audits. The risk- based approach to the audit programme preparation and delivery is thorough and flexible enough to respond to new risk information. The audit procedure used is comprehensive and supports the consistency and delivery of high-quality audits. The audits systematically address issues of compliance with planned arrangements, and the effective implementation and suitability of planned arrangements, and lead to generally sound conclusions and pertinent recommendations. The position of the Audit Unit within the organisation, however, is not optimal given that it is situated in a Directorate-General with another unit, instead of being directly subordinated to the Executive Director. A potential threat to the independence of the Audit Unit may arise if it is required to audit the activities of the second unit within the Directorate-General. In general it was found that the BFSA took action in the light of audit results and the positive impact of the audit activity on improving official controls could be demonstrated. The internal audit was accepted and appreciated by the auditees met. The audit system can ensure that the underlying causes of shortcomings are identified; however, given the nature of some of these shortcomings, it is difficult for these to be remedied through internal audit activity 29 alone. Notwithstanding the minor deficiencies identified, the audit arrangements that have been put in place by the BFSA address the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held with the BFSA and the MAFF on 5 October 2018. At this meeting the DG SANTE audit team presented their main findings and preliminary conclusions and confirmed the time limits for the production of the report and the competent authority response. The BFSA representatives accepted the conclusions presented by the audit team. The MAFF stated that it would provide more information regarding the audit arrangements relating to central level tasks and supervision of Control Bodies.

Ensure that the official veterinarians receive adequate training and equipment to enable them to a) carry out the controls on bait distribution as required by the Commission and b) implement the correct sampling for the monitoring and surveillance programmes. citations.text: Training of official staff does not meet the requirements laid down in Article 6(a) and (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In addition, official staff does not have the access to all appropriate equipment for carrying out controls laid down in Article 4(d) of the Regulation. This has had a negative impact both on the verification of vaccine bait distribution and on the monitoring of the effectiveness of vaccinations. In June 2018, the BFSA organised training for selected officials near the airfields on how to carry out, and report, the daily checks on storage temperatures, flight lines 3 and bait drops. However, the trainees were not equipped with adequate hardware, software or IT training to be able to carry out these controls in line with the requirements issued to Member States by the Commission in 2015 (finding 23). Prior to the annual hunting season, the BFSA issues instructions for sampling and sample submission procedures to the RFSDs. The instructions are the same to all RFSDs and cover sampling for both rabies surveillance (head only) and monitoring of bait uptake and sero-prevalence (head + blood/serum samples from foxes and golden jackals). As described elsewhere in this report (findings 31 and 54), several of the official veterinarians at local levels, who are responsible for the sampling and the sample submission, did not implement sampling in accordance with the instructions that the BFSA had issued to the RFSDs. Conclusions on competent authorities

Responsibilities are clearly assigned and national legislation and instructions provide a solid basis for the implementation of the rabies eradication programme. However, the official veterinarians responsible for the daily controls on the aerial distribution of vaccine baits has not received appropriate instructions, equipment or training to carry out these controls. Consequently, the competent authority cannot provide the guarantees required by the Commission that the aerial distribution of vaccine baits has been implemented as agreed in the approved eradication plan.

The training provided has not been sufficient to ensure that the official veterinarians collect and submit the correct samples from the two main categories of wild animals (passive surveillance and monitoring of the effectiveness of vaccination). This has led to inaccuracies in the overall assessments of the results of monitoring and rabies surveillance.

citations.text: Hunted foxes and golden jackals, as well as the occasional wolf, from areas outside the ORV areas are subject to rabies testing under a national active rabies surveillance programme. The BFSA has previously informed the Commission services that, until 2017 these tests were included in the applications for co-funding from the EU, but this would not be the case in the application for co-funding of the 2018 programme. In 2017, rabies tests were carried out under the national active surveillance programme on 444 foxes, 926 golden jackals and 1 wolf in total from 12 RFSDs outside the ORV area, and 2 hunted wolves from one RFSD within the ORV area. In 2018, the laboratory carried out rabies tests under the national active surveillance programme on 144 hunted foxes, 179 hunted golden jackals in total from 5 RFSDs outside the ORV area and five hunted wolves from one RFSD within the ORV area. In the 13 RFSDs (2018) where only part of the territory is covered by rabies vaccination, foxes and golden jackals hunted outside the ORV area have also been tested for rabies under the co-financed monitoring programme. 5.1.4 Verification of the monitoring and surveillance programmes

Each sample submission form indicates the geolocation of where the animal was shot or found. Neither the BFSA, nor the RFSD or the laboratory had used these data to indicate/determine if the tests carried out on the sample are eligible for co-funding under the monitoring programme or not. 14

The sampling for the monitoring of vaccine uptake and population immunity has improved since the previous audit. However, the uneven coverage, the lack of serological results from the regions added to the programme in 2018, the inclusion of samples from outside the vaccinated territories, the large proportion of golden jackals in the material and the deficiencies in the laboratory (see 5.4) weaken the reliability and representativeness of the results presented to the Commission.

There is a reasonable level of awareness among hunters but the authorities have made limited efforts to maintain a high awareness of rabies among the public, who might see rabies as a risk of the past. This is evident from the very few suspect cases and the limited numbers of samples submitted for passive surveillance to the local competent authorities. However, the passive surveillance has been under-reported by ca 50% to the Commission so the coverage has been better than reported, but it is still poor in certain important border areas where the competent authority considers the risk for incursion of rabies to be high. 15

The sample registration, and tests carried out, in the laboratory are sometimes not appropriate for the category of the sample due to a lack of clear categorisation of the samples on the submission form. Therefore, the summary results provided to the BFSA and the Commission have been misleading. The submission form used by the official veterinarians is the same irrespective of whether the sample is for the monitoring programme, for active surveillance outside the ORV area, or for the passive surveillance (suspect cases, animals killed in road traffic, animals found dead). A description of the sampled animal in free text on the submission form intends to guide the laboratory's classification of the sample. When official veterinarians had incorrectly submitted a blood sample (only required for the monitoring programme) with the animal's head (required for surveillance), the laboratory had handled the submission as if it belonged to the monitoring programme, also when the free text implied that it was not. There is no requirement for RFSDs with only part of their territory covered by ORV to indicate clearly if a sample originates from inside or outside of the ORV area. Consequently, the NRL has reported the results from animals hunted outside the vaccination area as if they belonged to the monitoring programme and were eligible for co-funding. Due to the miss-classification of passive surveillance samples, the NRL had not prioritised the samples for rapid rabies diagnostic tests, carried out over 100 unnecessary tests for biomarker and serology, and the total number of samples reported to the BFSA as passive surveillance was less than the actual numbers received and tested in the NRL.

Through the misclassification of samples and results, due to unclear information on the submission forms, the NRL has provided the competent authority with misleading results for rabies surveillance and monitoring of the effectiveness of the oral vaccination.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the laboratory has access to the products or services needed to carry out the tasks assigned to them. Article 101(3)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In 2017 and in 2019 (to date) the national reference laboratory for rabies (NRL) only tested less than half of the samples submitted for detection of antibodies. The NRL and the BFSA indicated that this problem had been linked to the procedures for procurement of test kits and was likely to continue into the next three-year period (2019-2021). In 2018, all 800 samples submitted for serological testing were analysed. In 2017, the NRL tested only 39% (317) of the 817 blood samples they had received. In 2019, the NRL tested the first 100 blood samples to arrive but samples arriving later have been stored frozen pending procurement of test kits. The laboratory expects that, although financial means have been made available in the budget,, the procurement rules may restrict the purchase to 900 tests, out of the ca 2,281 listed in the approved programme for 2019.

The basic methods of relevance for the rabies eradication programme are available in NRL. However, there is no confirmatory method for rabies, which is important e.g. if a person has been bitten by a potentially rabies-infected animal and the result of the initial FAT test of the biting animal is negative or inconclusive.

The FAT for rabies diagnosis and the tests for biomarker detection and age determination use methodology recommended by the EURL. However, the test used for detection of rabies antibodies is not the method recommended in international standards, has not been evaluated in international comparative tests, and does not meet the requirements in point (5)(f) of the Annex to Commission Decision 2008/341/EC. The acceptance criteria in the tender for purchase of ELISA kits for the detection of rabies antibodies are so specific that only the currently used commercial ELISA kit is eligible. The criteria include a requirement for validation for certain domestic species even though the NRL will use it for wildlife samples only. In published studies, the EURL and an OIE reference laboratory have shown that the commercially available ELISA used in the NRL is not sensitive enough and therefore not suitable for monitoring the effectiveness of rabies vaccination in foxes. A study from the EURL suggests that if this ELISA is used, the cut-off for deeming a test result positive needs to be lowered to increase the sensitivity of the method, compared to what is recommended in the instructions accompanying the test kit. The NRL has made no such adjustments to the method. 17 The performance of the commercial ELISA on sera from foxes had not been verified in the NRL, nor did the NRL take part in the 1st inter-laboratory study on rabies antibody detection in wildlife samples organised by the EURL in 2016. No information is available, from the manufacturer or from validation carried out in a manufacturer-independent laboratory, on the performance of this test on samples from golden jackals, which in 2018 represented 38% of the tested animals.

The NRL did not have sufficient test material to carry out serological analyses on a large proportion of the blood samples they received for the monitoring in 2017 and 2019. In addition, the low sensitivity of the serological method used in the NRL provides the competent authority with results that likely err towards a lower sero- prevalence in foxes(4). These weaknesses undermine the evaluation by the competent authority of the effect of the oral vaccination on the immunity of the target animal (fox) population. In addition, the laboratory does not have any confirmatory test method for rabies, which may delay important test results, especially in cases of suspect human exposure.

Despite the lack of sufficient supplies of test kits, the NRL used many of the available kits to analyse samples from golden jackals, a species for which the method's reliability is unknown. It is therefore not possible for the competent authority to investigate the possible reasons for the low sero-prevalence but high bait uptake reported by the NRL for golden jackals. 4 In their comments to the draft report the competent authority noted that in 2019 there is a new tender for diagnostic tests for serological analyses and FAT. 19

citations.text: Despite the above, the audit team noted in the holdings visited ­ which had been subject to official controls - that the records of these controls did not show that the following issues (which were seen by the audit team during the audit) had been identified: a. In two out of four holdings visited, operators had not: (i) recorded in holding registers, (ii) notified, and (iii) identified newborn calves; (for example, in one holding visited, 17 cows had 17 calves in the last 12 months, none of which had been registered). 6 b. In two out of four holdings visited, animals that had died on farm (fallen stock) and/or were emergency slaughtered had not been recorded as such in the holding register and thus appeared in the records as still "alive". c. In two out of four holdings visited, the number of animals in the registers did not reflect the actual number of animals on the holding.

In the holdings visited, the audit team noted that there had been significant delays in applying individual ear tags or retagging animals that had lost their identification, and there were frequent non-compliances with record keeping and reporting requirements. For example: a. Contrary to Article 4a of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 which requires identification of bovine animals within a maximum of 20 days from the birth of the animal and in any event before the animal leaves the holding on which it was born, in one of the holdings visited, six bovine animals out of 43 kept had no ear tags, and approximately 50% of those remaining ones had only one tag; b. Contrary to Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 - which requires that each animal keeper (except transporters) reports to the competent authority all movements to and from the holding and all births and deaths of animals in the holding, along with the dates of these events, within a period fixed by the Member State of between three and seven days of the event occurring - in three animal holdings visited, the keepers selling calves aged between one to two weeks old to other locations did not: (i) notify the birth of calves, (ii) record the birth and the sale in the holding registers, (iii) keep movement documents allowing to trace the calves to the holding of origin and link them with their mothers, and (iv) could not otherwise demonstrate that prior to movement, calves had been identified with individual ear tags. None of these non-compliances had been detected during the official controls on these holdings. The above-mentioned non-compliances with Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 in the holdings visited call into question the suitability and effectiveness of official controls and subsequent measures taken by the competent authorities. Another practical consequence is also a breach of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000. 5.2.3 Bovine passports

While checking the bovine identification documents in the visited premises, the audit team noted that there had been significant delays in issuing passports. In particular, in one of the slaughterhouses visited, bovine animals presented for slaughter were accompanied by passports that had been issued (for the first time) on the day prior to slaughter or on the day of slaughter. These animals were aged between 18 and 24 months. 7

The audit team analysed the data on the location and the number of bovine passports issued in comparison with the location and the number of registered new-born calves born in the country and noted a lack of correlation between the figures. In nine regions, differences between passports issued and animals born ranged from approximately 1,000 to almost 9,000. The officials in charge of conducting official controls did not pay attention to these discrepancies, which could indicate non-compliances related to animals' individual identification and movements, namely unregistered movements of unidentified young calves (see findings: 18.a, 24 and 25). 5.2.4 Computerised database

According to the data from VetIS, in the period from 2014 to 2018, the population of bovine animals has steadily increased from approximately 721,000 to 765,000. However, the audit team noted that there was a large cohort of bovine animals missing from the database. For example in 2018, the difference between the number of animals born and traded (into Bulgaria) and the number of animals slaughtered, dead, traded and exported (out of Bulgaria), resulted in a surplus of approximately 34,000 animals, without a known (confirmed) history (3). This represents approximately 4.5% of the bovine population in the country.

The owners of bovine holdings visited stated that their main activity is production of milk, and their cows calve every year. The audit team noted that except for two regions where the numbers of new-born calves registered in VetIS were plausible, in the remaining 26 regions registered calves represented from 17% to 30% of the expected number.

In one of the holdings visited, the owner stated that there were 17 calves born within the last 12 months ­ all were sold aged one to two weeks old. In another holding visited, the animal keeper confirmed that his cows calved annually and that he retained a few heifer calves for rebuilding the herd. The audit team cross-checked the situation on that holding with the VetIS data and noted that: a. The calf retained in the herd had no ear tags and was not identified by any other means. b. For 17 cows, ranging in age from 14 to 19 years old, only one to three calves per cow had been notified in VetIS during the entire cows' lives; the owner retained the notified calves in the herd, and during the audit they were presented as adult cows.

The BFSA has granted access to VetIS to officials from the central and regional level, official veterinarians in slaughterhouses and to registered veterinarians. One person at central level (VetIS administrator) has access to all the information, whilst other users are only allowed to see information limited to an individual animal or a holding. These users have limited possibilities to correct or edit data in the event they see a non-conformity. Slaughterhouse operators, those collecting and disposing of fallen stock and animal (3) Data by BFSA (VetIS) and from TRACES. 8 keepers, have no access to VetIS. The BFSA stated that it is preparing a new functionality for animal keepers to allow them to notify relevant events via smartphones and tablets.

In light of the above, VetIS does not meet the requirements of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 as it neither reflects the actual population of bovine animals in Bulgaria nor does it facilitate the supply of the required items of information set out in Article 14 of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.

While official controls on the identification and registration of bovine animals are carried out as planned and identified shortcomings are subsequently followed up, these controls have, to date, not identified some non-compliances related to the identification of bovine animals and notification of births of calves at holdings.

A lack of effective action by the competent authority to enforce the operators' obligations to notify all events at holdings has contributed to a situation where the information in the national database for registration and identification of bovine animals is unreliable. In addition, due to limitations in the database's functionality, information that would be relevant for the planning and implementation of official controls on BSE and ABP cannot be easily extracted. Overall, these deficiencies cumulatively undermine the reliability of the BSE monitoring programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all samples from bovine animals sent for BSE laboratory testing are correctly marked as to the identity of the sampled animal and are analysed in a timely fashion as required in Point 1 of Chapter C of Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the information provided by the competent authorities on monitoring in this sub-population is incomplete. There are significant discrepancies between the number of bovine animals from the sub-population of emergency slaughtered animals and found sick at ante mortem inspection reported by FCD and AHFCD (see Appendix, Tables 6 and 7). Data presented by FCD, AHFCD and those sourced from the BSE testing laboratories differ and cannot be reconciled (see Appendix, Tables 8 to 10, and Tables 16 to 18).

The audit team saw evidence of situations where cows emergency slaughtered at holdings had been classified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption. The opposite was the case in one of the BSE testing laboratories visited where all bovine animals sampled for BSE and notified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption had been reclassified by the laboratory to the sub-population of emergency slaughtered. In this laboratory, the approach has been in place for at least four years and concerned samples were collected from eight regions.

Due to the limited availability of testing kits, BFSA decided that samples collected from fallen bovine animals were of a low priority and delayed their testing. This resulted in a situation where samples from a group, which would ordinarily be considered as being a high risk (of BSE), were kept for several months before being tested (see findings 55 and 56).

The NRL-TSE is responsible for ensuring that there is a sufficient availability of BSE diagnostic tests for itself and for the regional BSE laboratories. The audit team noted that the arrangement for acquiring tests did not work effectively in 2018 as the regional laboratories and the NRL-TSE did not have sufficient tests available. This resulted in over 18,000 collected BSE samples (and an additional 11,000 for Scrapie) not being analysed. Due to this shortage of testing kits since August 2018, the samples from the sub- populations of bovine animals slaughtered at holdings as healthy, in emergency and dead were categorised as low priority and collected, but not tested. Only for the sub-population of healthy bovine animals slaughtered in slaughterhouses, have the laboratories carried out tests continuously without any interruption. In 2019, the BFSA outsourced the testing of stored samples to an external laboratory.

With respect to the arrangements for BSE testing, the audit team noted that the NRL-TSE did not overcome difficulties in ensuring availability of sufficient BSE test kits in 2019 and the backlog of untested samples is growing. At the time of this audit, there were 6,500 samples awaiting BSE testing (and 5,500 for Scrapie).

Samples of brainstem seen in the laboratories visited were placed in individual sampling containers, which were identified by either labels or a consecutive sequential number written with a marker. While the information from labels (date of slaughter, the 15 slaughterhouse number and the slaughter number of the animal or the ear tag number) could ensure traceability to the bovine animal sampled, the sole consecutive sequential number could not; especially if more samples with the same number were delivered for examination. This is not compliant with the provisions of Point 1 of Chapter C of Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, which requires that the samples should be marked correctly as to the identity of the sampled animal and Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requiring that samples must be handled and labelled in such a way as to guarantee both their legal and analytical validity.

The quality and quantity of samples, once collected, are able to ensure sufficient material for BSE testing. However, the method of identifying samples does not guarantee to trace back to the sampled animal in the event of a positive result.

Despite the fact that the NRL-TSE and regional BSE laboratories are accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, use the approved test kits listed in the Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and have performed satisfactorily in proficiency tests for BSE, both the competent authority and the NRL-TSE have consistently failed to ensure the availability of a sufficient number of diagnostic tests to analyse all the samples taken. This has resulted in an unsatisfactory situation where large numbers of samples from high-risk sub- 16 populations have either not been analysed or their analyses had been delayed for months, further weakening the reliability of the BSE monitoring results.

recommendations.text: To ensure compliance with the requirements laid down by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 concerning BSE monitoring of all eligible bovine animals from relevant sub-populations, and in accordance with Part I of Chapter A of Annex III to the said Regulatio to 84.

citations.text: The analysis of the available data on the sub-population of bovine animals slaughtered as healthy (aged over 30 months) (4), shows that: a. The number of BSE samples taken in slaughterhouses is lower than the number of healthy bovine animals eligible for BSE testing, and the discrepancy between these numbers is increasing (see Appendix, Table 1). b. The number of slaughterhouse samples tested for BSE is lower than the number of animals sampled. On average, approximately 30% of the samples taken have been tested (see Appendix, Table 2). c. A significant number of bovine animals is slaughtered at holdings and, in some years, the number of such animals is approximately double that slaughtered in slaughterhouses (see Appendix, Tables 3 and 4). d. The cumulative number of all healthy slaughtered bovine animals eligible for BSE testing, slaughtered both in slaughterhouses and at holdings, is much higher than the number of all tests actually carried out for this sub-population (see Appendix, Tables 4 and 5). The above findings are not in line with Point 2.2 of Part I of Chapter A to Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, which requires that all bovine animals slaughtered normally for human consumption as healthy and aged over 30 months are to be tested for BSE. 5.3.2 BSE monitoring in the sub-population of animals emergency slaughtered and found sick at ante mortem inspection

The audit team noted that the information provided by the competent authorities on monitoring in this sub-population is incomplete. There are significant discrepancies between the number of bovine animals from the sub-population of emergency slaughtered animals and found sick at ante mortem inspection reported by FCD and AHFCD (see Appendix, Tables 6 and 7). Data presented by FCD, AHFCD and those sourced from the BSE testing laboratories differ and cannot be reconciled (see Appendix, Tables 8 to 10, and Tables 16 to 18).

The audit team saw evidence of situations where cows emergency slaughtered at holdings had been classified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption. The opposite was the case in one of the BSE testing laboratories visited where all bovine animals sampled for BSE and notified as healthy/slaughtered for own consumption had been reclassified by the laboratory to the sub-population of emergency slaughtered. In this laboratory, the approach has been in place for at least four years and concerned samples were collected from eight regions.

The analysis of the available data on the sub-population of bovine animals, aged over 24 months, found sick at ante mortem inspection and emergency slaughtered shows that: a. The number of animals notified as emergency slaughtered and eligible for BSE testing is significantly higher for those slaughtered at holdings than in slaughterhouses (see Appendix, Table 11). A small proportion of these emergency slaughtered at holdings is reported in VetIS ­ again demonstrating the unreliability of the data in this system. b. Reporting on the number of animals found sick at ante mortem inspection is limited to one region, and even in this case the collected samples were not tested (see Appendix, Table 12.). c. The number of bovine animals from the sub-population of emergency slaughtered and found sick at ante mortem inspection reported as sampled is lower than the number of samples tested. The above findings are not in line with Point 2.1 of Part I of Chapter A to Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, which requires that all bovine animals, aged over 24 months old, emergency slaughtered and found sick at ante mortem inspection are to be tested for BSE. 5.3.3 BSE monitoring in the sub-population of dead animals (fallen stock)

The population of bovine animals aged over 30 months in the last five years in Bulgaria amounts to approximately 0.5 million heads (VetIS: 521,759 animals in 2018). In its TSE monitoring and eradication programme submitted to the Commission, the BFSA estimated that the number of fallen bovine animals eligible for BSE testing should amount to at least five thousand, representing 1% of this population. The audit team noted that apart from this estimate, there are no countrywide data on mortality at holdings and accordingly, the BFSA has no information on the number of bovine animals from the sub- population of dead bovine animals aged over 24 months. Thus, 12 the BFSA cannot verify if the number of collected samples reflects the entire sub- population eligible for testing (5).

The analysis of the available data on the sub-population of dead bovine animals eligible for BSE testing shows that: a. The number of fallen bovine animals reported as eligible for BSE testing is approximately 80 times lower than the amount estimated by the BFSA in its TSE monitoring and eradication programme, and is also much lower than the lowest average values from the EU statistics (see Appendix, Table 19). (5) The audit team requested information on the number of fallen bovine animals reported in VetIS but this information has not been provided. 13 b. The number of bovine animals sampled remains constantly low and until 2018, on average, represented 30% of the bovine animals collected as eligible for testing (see Appendix, Table 15). c. The number of samples tested does not match the number of the ones collected (see Appendix, Tables 14 and 15); moreover, there are significant delays in testing due to a shortage of test kits and assigning low priority to this sub-population (see findings 55 and 56). The above findings are not in line with Point 3.1 of Part I of Chapter A of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 which requires BSE testing of all dead bovine animals aged over 24 months (6). 5.3.4 BSE monitoring in the sub-population of BSE suspects

The samples are not taken from all animals that should be tested in the relevant sub- population. A significant proportion of eligible healthy bovine animals, mainly slaughtered outside slaughterhouses, which should have been tested for BSE, have not been sampled. Likewise, sampling of eligible animals emergency slaughtered or found sick at ante mortem inspection is limited to very few regions, whereas the majority of such animals have not been notified or sampled. In comparison with other Member States and even with the competent authority's own estimates, the number of fallen bovine animals sampled remains extremely low.

The audit team noted that, with regard to this recommendation: a. There had been no changes in the system of official controls on holdings aimed at addressing the issue of the BSE monitoring, in particular to verify that all eligible bovine animals from relevant sub-populations had been sampled and tested (one exception to this was the system put in place in one of the regions visited ­ see finding 29). Controls at holdings that would be relevant to verify the effectiveness of BSE monitoring are carried out in the framework of controls on animal identification. However, these do not cover aspects related to BSE monitoring (i.e. whether animals that had been slaughtered or died at holdings were eligible for sampling and testing). b. While collecting the BSE samples, the BFSA focuses on slaughterhouses. Sampling at holdings of all types from relevant sub-populations was inconsistently applied resulting in an underrepresentation of samples from eligible bovine animals that were slaughtered or died at holdings (see findings in section 5.3). c. Significant delays in testing samples from the risky sub-populations of bovines emergency slaughtered or found dead further undermine the effectiveness of the BSE monitoring programme (see conclusions in section 5.3). d. Official controls (through VetIS) on the work of registered veterinarians are almost non-existent, partially due to issues with the database's functionality and accuracy (see finding 27).

The audit team noted that, whilst the BFSA had issued practical guidance to animal keepers (8), none of the holdings visited had a container for collection of SRM or a (8) Available at: http://babh.government.bg/uploads/File/Zdraveopazvane/Zarazni_bolesti/TSE/13_Luda%20krava- praktichesko%20rakovodstvo%20za%20fermerite.pdf 20 separate, dedicated place for storage of dead animals. These deficiencies had neither been noted by the competent authority in the reports of their official controls nor resulted in any measures being taken.

The CAs have not demonstrated that they have put in place actions that would effectively address recommendation 4 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944. This additionally undermines Bulgaria's request for a relaxation of the frequency of testing for BSE.

The implementation of the actions to address recommendation 6 of audit report DG(SANCO)2011-8944 has not been effective. Collection of SRM produced as a result of on-farm slaughtering of bovine animals in backyard holdings continues to be inexistent.

recommendations.text: To take targeted action to enforce compliance with Union animal identification and registration rules within the pig sector, focusing particularly on non-commercial holdings. · Article 17 of Decision 2014/709/EU · Articles 4(1) and 5(1)(a) of Directive 2008/71/EC · Articles 54 and 55 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004

citations.text: Backyard holdings are legally obliged to register and the authorities highlighted this requirement during an awareness campaign. At the time of the audit, only a small percentage complied with this requirement. All 24 backyard holdings where outbreaks (1) In their response to the draft report, the BFSA noted that Ordinance No 44 had already been amended as of January 2020 and is in force. It allows non-commercial holdings to keep up to three fattening pigs, and provides for a range of biosecurity requirements for each pig farm category. 4 have been detected up to 3 October 2019, were not registered. In one region visited, nine backyard holdings registered after an awareness campaign, but a census carried out in the region revealed 505 backyard holdings, keeping 919 pigs. One backyard farmer visited expressed certain reluctance, as this would imply costs for the registration, for ear tags and a compulsory contract with a veterinarian. The competent authorities declared the costs as being very low and explained a certain general reluctance of backyard farmers to comply with the registration requirements. Competent authorities do not grant unregistered holdings compensation in the case of depopulation in order to motivate the farmers to register.

By decision of Central Epizootic Council, the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Forestry (MAFF), took up this initiative in the summer of 2019 and sent out a letter to the Governors to be implemented in their respective regions. The authorities asked keepers of backyard holdings situated in a 20 km radius of industrial holdings, slaughterhouses, main roads and in areas defined as high-risk to voluntarily slaughter their pigs early and before the end of August 2019. They also asked the keepers to sign declarations that they would not replace the pig for at least one year and that they would disinfect their holdings. In return, they received compensation of 300 Leva (approximately 150 Euro) for cleaning and disinfection activities per holding. Official veterinarians from other RFSD checked a sample of 15 % of the backyard holdings to verify compliance with this requirement. In the region mentioned above, 797 farmers signed the mentioned declaration.
Nearly all regions in Bulgaria implemented this campaign: 31,242 backyard holdings stopped keeping pigs and approximately 50,000 pigs were slaughtered.

The owner of one backyard holding visited, which had been affected by ASF, admitted to the following non-compliances: a. no registration of the holding; b. no identification of animals, no register of pigs kept; c. keeping a sow for breeding; d. movement of animals without notification (boar of neighbouring holding for insemination); e. swill feeding; 5 f. no notification of the registered veterinarian within 24 hours of the change of the status of the animals (including home-slaughter), although this is required under national law. In general, the competent authorities reported frequent and major non-compliances in the unregistered backyard holdings, which they identified during the census.

In one region, RFSD highlighted that registered veterinarians authorised to register holdings and who had been contacted by farmers willing to register their holdings did not register the holding nor did they encourage farmers to register. Private veterinarians providing services to unregistered holdings do not inform the veterinary authorities on the existence of the holdings.

In one region visited, the competent authority informed about a holding where four wild boar are kept for training hunting dogs. Under the current legislation, dog-training areas do not have to be registered as a pig holding, which represents a weakness in the control of all pig holdings by the competent authority.

Despite a legal requirement and an intensive awareness campaign since 2015, only a limited number of non-commercial holdings are registered which makes it difficult for the authorities to detect promptly the disease and to control its spread. The proactive measures taken by the authorities to depopulate backyard holdings in high-risk areas are likely to significantly reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread. However, there is uncertainty about how this limitation of the risk will be maintained when the defined period for the non-population expires, and about how the authorities will monitor these holdings in particular when they are going to restock.

Private registered veterinarians are complicit in maintaining the unregistered pig population as they do not actively support the registration of non-commercial holdings but rather continue to provide service to unregistered holdings.

Two positive cases of ASF were confirmed in pigs that had been dumped on a public road; the origin of these pigs could not be traced. When the campaign for the early slaughter of pigs in non-commercial holdings was initiated in the summer of 2019, MAFF ordered a permanent supervision of slaughterhouses by the veterinary authorities in cooperation with the police forces in order to avoid an illegal commercial slaughter of pigs from unregistered holdings. 5.4.3 Wild boar

Despite the recent efforts to reduce the number of non-commercial holdings and to bring them into compliance with biosecurity requirements, it is very likely that there still exits a considerable number of unregistered backyard holdings in the country. The absence of reliable data on the location and movement of pigs within the non-commercial sector means that it is often not possible to trace animals that could have carried ASF virus to or from outbreak holdings. It also means that it is difficult for the veterinary authorities to enforce the prohibition to dispatch live pigs originating from the areas included in the Part III territory in the case of non-commercial holdings. This surely contributes to the spread of the disease and makes its containment very difficult.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the biosecurity measures as laid down in Ordinance No 44 of 20 April 2006 of MAFF, Order PR 11-1813 of the BFSA and the eradication plan for ASF in wild boar, approved by the Decision (EU) 2019/484 are implemented in both commercial and non-commercial holdi

citations.text: According to national legislation (Ordinance No 44 of 20 April 2006), pig holdings are categorised according to their size and biosecurity standards. Commercial holdings with high biosecurity standards include industrial holdings and family farms type "A" holdings. In addition, some outdoor farms in the Eastern part of the country raise free- roaming East Balkan pigs, a local breed. The current legislation allows non-commercial holdings to keep up to five pigs for own consumption, but not breeding sow or boars. This classification is broadly in line with the ASF strategy of the EU. (1) Type of pig holding Number of holdings as Number of pigs of September 2019 Industrial 65 538,000 Family farm type "A" 192 30,000 East Balkan pig 46 3,600

The owner of one backyard holding visited, which had been affected by ASF, admitted to the following non-compliances: a. no registration of the holding; b. no identification of animals, no register of pigs kept; c. keeping a sow for breeding; d. movement of animals without notification (boar of neighbouring holding for insemination); e. swill feeding; 5 f. no notification of the registered veterinarian within 24 hours of the change of the status of the animals (including home-slaughter), although this is required under national law. In general, the competent authorities reported frequent and major non-compliances in the unregistered backyard holdings, which they identified during the census.

Officials use a specific checklist to verify the level of biosecurity of the commercial holdings. The requirements, which the officials have to check, are broadly in line with those established in the strategic approach to the management of ASF for the EU. The authorities indicated the following key findings: a. The level of biosecurity in industrial holdings was, in general, quite good, but there are numerous backyard holdings in close proximity to industrial holdings; b. Non-compliances with certain biosecurity requirements, e.g. the structure of the buildings and the installations were not in line with established standards, but mainly with regard to operational measures, e.g. weak record keeping of visitors, no clear distinction within the holding of "clean" and "dirty" sections.

The authorities introduced additional biosecurity measures pursuant to order PR 11- 1813 of the BFSA as of 30 August 2019 in light of the evolution of the disease. They also prepared awareness material targeted at family farms and backyard holdings. Those additional measures included a ban on live pigs markets in the whole country and a ban on pork meat sale in farmers markets. 5.1.2 Wild boar

The competent authorities have issued stricter operational rules in order to rectify shortcomings in the biosecurity rules in commercial holdings. These would likely further increase the level of biosecurity.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, for each outbreak of ASF, an epidemiological inquiry is carried out as required by Article 8 of Directive 2002/60/EC.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed the epidemiological inquiries carried out for several outbreaks. In the industrial holdings, the veterinary authorities had investigated the possible sources of infection to or from the holdings to a certain extent, but in most cases had not finalised the epidemiological inquiry, and the cause for the infection was not really followed up. The authorities indicated that this was due to time constraints, i.e. the fact that they were involved in depopulation activities and several other outbreaks. In the backyard holdings, the competent authorities focused on the depopulation of unregistered holdings in the protection zones rather than on determining the cause for the infection.

The lack of thorough epidemiological inquiries, and the fact that due to time constraints the staff are faced with they were not able to finalise epidemiological investigations in commercial holdings, means that opportunities are missed to intercept possible transmission of the virus via vectors or fomites or contaminated products to previously uninfected areas

recommendations.text: To verify whether the veterinary measures taken with regard to the eradication of ASF, in particular on the establishing of the restriction zones and surveillance activities in the domestic pig and wild boar population, have been implemented. Article 8(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The agreement between the veterinary authorities and the EFA, together with the enforcing support of EFA and the application of innovative measures such as trapping and silent hunt out of the season is likely to reduce the density of the wild boar 9 population and thus to help slowing down the transmission of ASF from it. However, the lack of systematic checks by the veterinary authorities prevents the authorities to demonstrate that the measures are in fact implemented as planned.

The veterinary authorities do not receive regularly the information from EFA on the numbers of wild boar shot and therefore they cannot check the hunting records against the sample submission records to determine whether all hunted wild boar have in fact been tested for ASF. The obligation to use the hunting module (see finding 36) in the hunting season 2019/2020 within the infected area should provide information about all wild boar shot and allow a crosscheck on the number of wild boar sampled. 5.2.3 Laboratory network

In the case of one outbreak, the BFSA established surveillance zone restrictions on a pig fattening holding located at a distance of 7.2 km in a straight line from the outbreak. This decision was subsequently re-assessed by the RFSD and BFSA headquarters. The reassessment took into account that the fattening holding was located in a different municipality and that the distance by road to the outbreak was 12, 5 km. On this basis, the RFSD decided to lift the restrictions four days later. This decision was not in line with the requirements set out in Article 9 of Directive 2002/60/EC, which requires the surveillance zone to cover all holdings within a "radius of at least 10 kilometres". During the period when other pig holdings within the surveillance zone remained under restriction, this fattening holding was allowed to slaughter pigs in a slaughterhouse located in the same region and the meat was placed on the national market. However, the holding was subject to official supervision with the collection and testing of samples to rule out ASF presence before it was allowed to resume normal trading. In addition, during the lifting of the restrictions in the 10 km surveillance zone, samples for ASF were taken on this fattening holding with a negative result.

The central veterinary authorities have established a clear chain of command that is supported by written instructions, regular trainings and meetings and reporting arrangements, in line with Annex VI(c) of Directive 2002/60/EC. RFSDs have to report on a weekly basis to the BFSA on the measures taken with regard to ASF eradication. While BFSA staff are regularly present in the regions during the confirmation of positive cases, they do not systematically supervise the regions to verify the correct implementation of instructions.

The authorities at central level do not carry out a systematic supervision of the implementation of measures related to ASF control neither on veterinary authorities nor with regard to the requirements in hunting grounds. Therefore, they do not become aware of shortcomings in the implementation of measures and cannot correct them. (5)

audits.title: Official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that documented procedures and arrangements for the performance of official controls are in place, and that they have been updated as appropriate.

citations.text: The BFSA stated that, with limited exceptions, it did not have documented procedures in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods of animal origin entering the EU, including on transhipped consignments, consignments in transit and channelling of consignments, which is not in line with article 12(1) of the OCR.

The limited exceptions concern a documented procedure for the use of TRACES-NT in the case of unsatisfactory laboratory results for certain consignments of goods of animal origin, and a standard operating procedure for the sampling of food of animal origin, the latter of which the audit team noted had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR.

In contrast to finding 15, the BFSA has documented procedures in place for official controls on food of non-animal origin entering the EU, for the onward transportation and transfer to control points of consignments of food and feed of non-animal origin, and for the exchange of information in iRASFF, which is in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. A further procedure concerning the action to take for non-compliant consignments of (8) https://btsfacademy.eu/training/ 6 food of non-animal origin and food contact materials had not been updated as appropriate in line with Article 12(3)(b) of the OCR.

The BFSA also stated there are no documented arrangements in place for the implementation of measures on consignments of animals and goods referred to in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR, which is not in line with Article 12(1) and Article 64(3)(d) of the OCR.

Whilst there is a framework in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, underpinned by systematic communication and cooperation between the relevant authorities, certain organisational aspects weaken the effectiveness of the control system. These include the lack of (updated) documented procedures and arrangements and the failure to develop and implement an appropriate monitoring plan. It is likely that the shortfall in the implementation of control verification procedures hindered the ability of the competent authority to identify and address those shortcomings. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

recommendations.text: To ensure that a monitoring plan is developed to implement the detailed rules for physical checks on goods of animal origin subject to official controls at border control posts, and that samples are taken and analysed in accordance with that plan.

citations.text: The BFSA Border Control Directorate stated that it develops an annual risk-based monitoring plan for official controls on products of animal origin for human consumption entering the EU, as part of its National Monitoring Programme for the Control of Residues of Veterinary Medicinal Products and Environmental Contaminants in Live Animals and Products of Animal Origin 2021 (hereafter `National Monitoring Programme'). The monitoring plan does not include products of animal origin which are not intended for human consumption, or hazards other than residues and histamine. The BFSA informed the audit team that it has established a working group to review the scope of the monitoring plan for 2022, which it expects to be finalised by 31 March 2022.

The BFSA stated that in 2021 no samples were taken at BCPs under the monitoring plan for 2021 due to a significant delay in the approval of the National Monitoring Programme by MAFF. The programme was finally approved on 31 October 2021 and as a result, the BSFA stated that the sampling and analysis included in the monitoring plan for 2021 would be carried out over a limited period, between 1 January and 1 April 2022 only. Up to 8 February 2022, 47 out of 102 planned samples had been taken at the BCPs.

The audit team noted that the monitoring plan as developed and implemented did not achieve the objective of monitoring the conformity of goods of animal origin entering the EU with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of the OCR, and in particular of detecting hazards. This is not in line with Article 4(5) and point 5 of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

Whilst there is a framework in place for the conduct of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, underpinned by systematic communication and cooperation between the relevant authorities, certain organisational aspects weaken the effectiveness of the control system. These include the lack of (updated) documented procedures and arrangements and the failure to develop and implement an appropriate monitoring plan. It is likely that the shortfall in the implementation of control verification procedures hindered the ability of the competent authority to identify and address those shortcomings. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON ANIMALS AND GOODS ENTERING THE EU

recommendations.text: To ensure that the specific rules for official controls of consignments of goods of animal origin in transit are implemented, in particular that the consignments leave in vehicles or transport containers sealed by the authority at the border control post of introduction into the EU; and that the competent authorities of the border control post of introduction verify with the competent authorities at the place of destination whether or not the consignment has arrived in cases where confirmation of its arrival has not been received within a period of 15 days from the date on which transit was authorised.

citations.text: The audit team evaluated three CHED-Ps authorised for transit of consignments of animal origin and noted that each consignment was subjected to a documentary and identity check, however in all cases the identity check consisted only of a check of the seals on the containers or means of transport, despite the accompanying official certificate not providing information on those seals. This is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. Those consignments also left the BCP of introduction without the vehicles or transport containers being sealed by the competent authority, which is not in line with Article 19(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The BFSA stated that BCP staff relied on the seals applied by Customs.

The audit team further noted that, 106 out of 2 131 transiting consignments in 2020, and 1 604 out of 4 210 in 2021, had been recorded in TRACES-NT without confirmation of arrival and compliance of the consignment at the BCP of exit within a period of 15 days from the date on which the transit was authorised. In 2020, the majority of BCPs of exit were located in Bulgaria (64 out of 106), whereas in 2021, the majority were located in other Member States (1 513 out of 1 604). The BFSA confirmed to the audit team that the BCP staff at the BCPs of introduction in Bulgaria do not systematically follow-up with the competent authorities of the BCPs of exit (either in Bulgaria or in other Member States) on consignments for which Part III of the CHED has not been completed. This is not in line with Article 20(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. However, the BSFA stated that, in each case, it contacts Customs to confirm that the transiting consignments have left the EU, examples of which were provided to the audit team.

Whilst consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, which are generally carried out in line relevant EU legislation, shortcomings in their implementation, particularly concerning transits, the performance of identity checks on goods of animal origin and the recording of the outcome of the official controls performed, and any decisions taken, in the CHED, collectively undermine the overall effectiveness of the control system to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU.

citations.text: The audit team further noted that in the case of the BCPs Kapitan Andreevo and Kalotina, the BCP facilities for controls of animals entering the EU are used for the performance of official controls on consignments of animals intended for export from the EU. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control point plans.

citations.text: In all of the establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection/audit reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in five of the seven establishments. In general, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was deficient or very generic without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assessment. This issue was not reflected in any of the inspection/audit reports seen and operators were thus, unaware that there was a problem. Having said this, some of the inspectors did correctly identify these deficiencies during the interviews. 4

Planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and allows for official controls to be carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. Implementation of inspections was, however, not effective. The audit team identified shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, (ii) operators' testing on cross-contamination, (iii) operators' traceability systems and (iv) operators' compliance with labelling requirements. These shortcomings in implementation weaken the effectiveness of the overall feed control system. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the staff carrying out official sampling apply practices ensuring legal, scientific and technical validity of the official feed samples taken.

citations.text: The audit team observed official sampling at the three compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In addition, a number of sampling records from 2019 and onwards were scrutinised. Based on these, the audit team made the following observations: · In two of the three establishments a substantial part of the batch suggested for sampling was not accessible. Therefore, it was impossible to collect incremental samples representatively 7 from the batch. The inspectors collected the incremental samples only from a part of the batch (i.e. sampled portion). The inspectors did not identify the size of the sampled portion and consequently did not record it on the sampling protocol. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in part 10 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. · In one establishment, the size of each incremental sample was less than 100 g which is not in line with the requirements laid down in part 9.2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. · In one establishment, the number of incremental samples collected was lower than the minimum required in part 5.1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. · In one establishment, two final samples were prepared which is not in line with the requirements laid down in part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

Notwithstanding the risk-based approach adopted for the planning of official sampling and the fact that the laboratories used for testing are accredited, appropriately designated and operate effective quality control, significant shortcomings in the implementation of sampling and testing substantially undermine the legal and technical validity of the samples and reliability of decisions made on the basis of results. Cumulatively these shortcomings weaken the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

The audit team scrutinised a substantial number of analytical tests (with related raw data) and reports related to undesirable substances within the meaning of Directive 2002/32/EC and observed that, when relevant, the results were recalculated to a feed with a moisture content of 12% and that the expanded measurement uncertainty was properly reported. However, in the vast majority of the reports seen, the analytical recovery was not indicated and it was unclear whether the result(s) had been corrected for recovery. recommendations.text: To ensure that the designated competent authority or authorities organise and perform the official controls on bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods at primary production prescribed in EU legislatio

citations.text: Bulgaria has not fixed the location and boundaries of production areas, contrary to Article 52(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The BFSA stated that each mussel farm is considered as an individual production area, and that the BFSA's Directorate of Animal Health and Welfare has a register of mussels' aquaculture farms publicly available at the BFSA website, with the farm location and boundaries coordinates provided by the Black Sea Basin Directorate.

Bulgaria has not carried out the sanitary surveys required in Article 56 of the same Regulation. Consequently, it has not classified them, contrary to the requirements of Articles 52(2) and (3) of the same Regulation.

At the time of the audit, there was no monitoring of production areas (or aquaculture farms if they are individually considered, see paragraph 4) for microbiological, chemical contaminants, biotoxins or phytoplankton, contrary to the requirements of Articles 57 to 61 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Consequently, there is neither management of production areas nor record and exchange of information to interested parties, which conditions are established respectively in Articles 61 and 62, and 66 of the same Regulation, with the exception of the BFSA's register of mussels' aquaculture farms (see paragraph 4), which could partially meet the recording of information required in Article 66(a) of that Regulation.

As required by Article 64 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the BFSA has in place a sampling programme of final products of bivalve molluscs' origin, either at establishments or at retail level. Official samples of mussels and wedge clams are tested for biotoxins at the NRL and for E. coli and salmonella at the regional official control laboratories. Non- compliant results trigger the recall and withdraw from the market of the batch of bivalve molluscs tested. 5.2.2 Official controls of certain bivalve molluscs harvested outside classified production areas
Bulgaria does not carry out the controls of rapana seasnail required by Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. 5.2.3 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

As explained in paragraph 2, the Executive Agency for Fisheries and Aquaculture carries out official controls in the field of fisheries policy, including for the movement of fishery product from fishing grounds. For this, it has prepared a template with all the information that operators have to fill out for every catch, and it issues pads of individually numbered documents to each operator. In the case of aquaculture mussels, wedge clams and rapana seasnail, the information contained in this document meets the relevant requirements of Chapter I (3) and (4) of Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) 853/2004. Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs

There is no system of official controls of bivalve molluscs and marine gastropods at primary production level in Bulgaria and the majority of the requirement of EU legislation are not met. Although there are certain official controls in place after primary production (carried out at establishments), they are insufficient to provide adequate food safety assurances if the primary production is not controlled. 5

audits.title: evaluate emergency preparedness in the plant health sector

recommendations.text: Ensure that the PPQCFFV Directorate and the CLPQ have a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff so that legally required work on surveys and contingency plans can be performed efficiently and effectively as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The PPQCFFV Directorate and the CLPQ do not have a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff in the area of plant health as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The BFSA stated that there are five staff in the PPQCFFV Directorate and 21 staff in the CLPQ dealing with plant health, with 64 plant health inspectors in the 28 RFSDs. The BFSA noted that the number of staff dealing with plant health matters had halved in the previous ten years, despite an increase in the workload. These numbers include both technical and administrative staff and include staff responsible for implementing all aspects of plant health legislation. The BFSA gave concrete examples where the lack of staff, and in particular the lack of experienced staff, means that legal requirements are not being met. These examples are described in this report and include: · the incomplete nature of multi-annual survey programmes (findings 13 and 15), · the lack of statistically based surveys for X. fastidiosa (finding 17), · the vast majority of survey results for Union quarantine pests not being provided to the Commission and to other MS (finding 32), · delays in developing contingency plans and the lack of detail in these plans (findings 38 and 41).

Limited staff resources in the PPQCFFV Directorate and in the CLPQ, compounded by IT related inefficiencies, mean that a number of legal obligations are not respected ­ the most important of which are determining which Union quarantine pests should be surveyed when developing multi-annual survey programmes, and developing sufficiently detailed contingency plans for all relevant priority pests.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the BFSA has appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment to ensure that staff can perform official controls and other official activities effectively and efficiently as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The BFSA does not have appropriate and properly maintained Information Technology (IT) facilities and equipment as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. It has not had an IT system to plan and to record all plant health survey activity since 2007. Instead, information on each survey is recorded in each RFSD using spreadsheets. This information is subsequently compiled by the relevant report rapporteur for priority pests or the PPQCFFV Directorate for other pests. For example, S. frugiperda is surveyed under three separate annual survey programmes ­ for vegetables, for ornamental plants, and for other plants. The resulting data from each of these three surveys is compiled separately in each of the 28 RFSDs, and subsequently reported to the single rapporteur charged with compiling this into a single dataset at national level. The cumbersome and time-consuming nature of this procedure makes it very inefficient to compile survey results and to report these results to the Commission, with the result that less than 20% of all surveys are reported to the Commission.

Limited staff resources in the PPQCFFV Directorate and in the CLPQ, compounded by IT related inefficiencies, mean that a number of legal obligations are not respected ­ the most important of which are determining which Union quarantine pests should be surveyed when developing multi-annual survey programmes, and developing sufficiently detailed contingency plans for all relevant priority pests.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all Union quarantine pests are either included in, or excluded with a justification from, the multi-annual survey programme, as required by Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031

citations.text: Under the 2021-2023 programme, the BFSA planned and conducted surveys on 155 pests, comprising 18 priority pests and 137 Union quarantine pests, under a range of crop-specific surveys. The remaining Union quarantine pests (more than 240) were neither included in, nor excluded with a justification from, the programme, which is not in compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

As was the case for the 2021-2023 programme, 240 or more Union quarantine pests are neither included in, nor excluded with a justification from, the 2024-2028 multi-annual survey programme, which is not in compliance with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The multi-annual survey programme for 155 Union quarantine pests (including 18 priority pests) provides a sound basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. However, at least two thirds of Union quarantine pests, some of which could establish in Bulgaria, are not surveyed, giving rise to the risk that some of these pests could establish, and remain undetected until such time as their eradication would be impossible.

recommendations.text: Ensure that in cases where Union quarantine pests are excluded from multi- annual survey programmes, that the justifications for exclusion are in line with Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: Thirty-seven pests are excluded from the 2024-2028 multi-annual survey programme with a clear justification. In the majority of these cases, the justification relates to the ecoclimatic conditions or to the absence of the host species as permitted under Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, in 40% of cases, the justification is either that official controls take place at the point of import, or that there is a proposal to deregulate the pest, or that the risk of the pest establishing in Bulgaria is low, none of which are permitted as valid reasons for excluding pests from multi-annual survey programmes under Article 22(1) of that Regulation. 6 5.2.2 Planning annual statistically based survey programmes for priority pests

recommendations.text: Establish and implement a statistically based annual survey programme for Xylella fastidiosa each year as required by Article 2(4) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201.

citations.text: Bulgaria did not establish (i.e. did not plan to conduct) a statistically based survey programme for X. fastidiosa in 2023 and 2024 as required by Article 2(4) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201, primarily due to a lack of human resources. However, some requirements laid down in Article 2 of this Regulation are complied with in the annual survey programmes for X. fastidiosa, as described in findings 21, 22 and 23. 5.2.3 Planning annual risk-based survey programmes for priority pests

The implementation of the annual risk-based survey programme for priority pests provides a high level of assurance that any outbreaks of these pests will be detected promptly. However, the failure to develop the required statistically based annual survey programme for X. fastidiosa means that the level of confidence the current risk-based survey programme for this pest provides is unknown.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the results for all Union quarantine pests surveyed each year are reported to the Commission and to other MS by 30 April of the following year, as required by Article 22(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 12(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 and Article 35(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201.

citations.text: Bulgaria generally reports the results of the annual surveys of priority pests to the Commission and to other MS, by the deadline of 30 April for the preceding year as required by Article 24(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 2(8) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 regarding X. fastidiosa and Article 12(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 as regards S. frugiperda. In 2022 and 2023, Bulgaria reported results on 23 and 28 of the 137 pests surveyed to the Commission and to other MS, which is not in line with Article 22(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The BFSA attributed the failure to report results for the vast majority of Union quarantine pests surveyed to difficulties in compiling and aggregating survey data, as described in finding 5. 9 Conclusions on survey programmes

The failure to report survey results for the vast majority of Union quarantine pests surveyed each year means that this important information is not easily accessible to the Commission and to other MS.
