recommendations.text: Ensure that: · all required contingency plans are drawn up and kept up to date, and communicated to the Commission and to other MS, as required by Arti- cle 25(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, · all relevant stakeholders are consulted when drawing up and keeping up to date contingency plans as required by Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, · each contingency plan contains sufficient detail regarding CAs' access to laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise and resources nec- essary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, con- tainment of the priority pest concerned as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: Bulgaria has drawn up pest-specific contingency plans for 11 of the 15 priority pests which are capable of entering into and becoming established in its territory. These plans were communicated to the Commission and to other MS as required by Article 25(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 by uploading them to internet Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF) plant health portal on 26 August 2024, some eight months after the legal deadline. The BFSA stated that work was ongoing on one of the four remaining 10 required plans at the time of the audit in September 2024, but acknowledged that there was no clear time schedule to conclude this work. Finally, it acknowledged that it had not consulted all relevant stakeholders when drawing up contingency plans as required by Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Therefore, Bulgaria had not drawn up contingency plans for all priority pests capable of entering into and becoming established in its territory by 14 December 2023 as required by Article 25(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 4(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 as regards S. frugiperda and Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 as regards X. fastidiosa. The BFSA explained that this delay occurred due to a lack of human resources.

The published contingency plans all share a common format. The audit team examined the contingency plans for S. frugiperda and X. fastidiosa as a representative sample. Based on this examination, the plans comply with most, but not all, requirements of Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 4(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 and Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. Specifically, the plans lack sufficient detail regarding CAs' access to laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise and resources necessary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of the priority pest concerned as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

Bulgaria is not sufficiently prepared to eradicate outbreaks of priority pests. Of the 15 required contingency plans, four remain to be drafted, with no clear deadline for their completion, while the published contingency plans lack the necessary detail to help the authorities rapidly and effectively eradicate any established priority pests. 11

citations.text: Applications for the authorisation of a PPP may be submitted at any given time, unless when Bulgaria is requested to act as the zonal rapporteur Member State pursuant to Article 33(2)(b) and Article 35 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Such applications are only accepted once the RACFC has the necessary resources to conduct the evaluations. This is not in line with Article 33(1) and Article 35 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.
The chronic staff shortages faced by RACFC prevent Bulgaria from serving effectively as the rapporteur MS for zonal authorisations and may dissuade applicants from applying there.

recommendations.text: To ensure that emergency authorisations are granted: a) on the basis of a single use b) only when the danger they address cannot be contained, at least in the medium term, by other reasonable means, including the extension of the authorisation of PPPs already authorised, c) where appropriate measures are taken to ensure consumer safety in accordance with Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009

citations.text: Emergency authorisations pursuant to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 are also managed by the BFSA, through the Council of PPPs, with the Executive Director of BFSA serving as the ultimate authority for authorisation. A designated department within BFSA, along with another from the RACFC, is responsible for determining whether the specific conditions for such authorisations have been fulfilled. However, the risk evaluators from RACFC are not engaged in this process and a simple declaration by the applicant, often citing an existing authorisation in another Member State, is considered adequate. The audit team considers that this may not always be 6 adequate to ensure the consumer safety referred to in Article 53(1) of the mentioned regulation.

The majority of emergency authorisations each pertain to several uses beyond the existing authorisation for already authorised PPPs. The audit team considered, especially when contemplating the issuance of repeated emergency authorisations, that these applications would be better accommodated through label extension within the conventional authorisation framework, for each one of the uses within those bundles, thereby maintaining the system's integrity, as referred to in Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20093. Conclusions on authorisation of plant protection products

Regarding applications of emergency authorisations under Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, the risk assessment authority is not involved, which may make it difficult to guarantee that adequate measures are taken to ensure consumer safety.
It is a policy of BFSA that one emergency authorisation may include multiple crops and/or targets. This is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009 for emergency authorisations.

Furthermore, emergency authorisations commonly involve authorised PPPs. The dangers these authorisations are addressing could therefore be contained by other means, namely through authorisation extensions of those PPPs, according to Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system.

recommendations.text: To ensure that unacceptable co-formulants, as defined by Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, and impurities subject to conditions and restrictions, as defined by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EU) 1107/2009, are covered by the accreditation scope of a laboratory designated to carry out formulation analyses of PPPs, as laid down by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The Central Laboratory for Chemical Testing and Control is designated for performing formulation analyses of PPPs. It is accredited under ISO 17025/2018 with a flexible accreditation scope and engages in inter-laboratory comparisons with other MS. The analyses focus primarily on identifying the content of active substances and certain physical and chemical properties of PPPs. A complete formulation analysis of a PPP has only been done once in recent years. Thus, the analysis programme does generally not cover co-formulants and impurities found in active substances. Consequently, CAs lack the means to confirm the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs, as stated in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and they are unable to determine whether certain impurities do not exceed the maximum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances, as required by Article 6(b) of that Regulation. 12 Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls.

The effectiveness of the control system in guaranteeing that the PPPs placed on the market are in conformity with their compositional specifications as stated in their authorisation is compromised by the lack of testing for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities within the sampling programme.

In particular, effective enforcement of requirements regarding the labelling of PPPs should be ensured by providing further guidance and instructions on this matter to the inspectors.

citations.text: Authorisations of PPPs requiring critical label amendments (such as deletion of uses, reduction of doses, and introduction of special risk mitigation measures), resulting from recent and similarly critical regulatory restrictions on their active substances, have been properly and promptly revised. Nevertheless, the audit team noted inadequacies in the official inspections to verify and enforce the implementation of such label updates (see finding 54). 5.1.5. Low-risk substances and candidates for substitution

However, there is no guidance provided for inspectors on how to prioritise their inspection. In all the inspections observed by the audit team, the detailed examination of labels was carried out on PPPs selected at random. Generally, official controls on the marketing of PPPs are carried out consistently and at an appropriate frequency as per the annual national schedule. audits.title: Slaughter hygiene and meat inspection requirements

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that official controls are performed in accordance with documented procedures, which shall contain instructions for staff performing official controls as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The CCA has not issued instructions or standard procedures covering the technical as- pects within the scope of this audit. For the official controls at slaughterhouses, there are no guidance/instructions on ante-mortem inspections (AMI), on animal welfare controls and on the verification of food business operators' (FBOs) self-control systems. The cur- rent instructions on post-mortem inspection (PMI), have not been updated to take into account the last changes in EU legislation. During the visits at the slaughterhouses the audit team noted that the official controls were not effective and there is no consistency in the way they are carried out (see paragraphs 28, 30, 33, 36, 38, 45, 50 and 52).

The official control system is supported by national legislation covering the relevant as- pects within the scope of the audit. However, the absence of guidance docu- ments/instructions for the official staff compromises the guarantees that official controls are effective and are carried out in a uniform and consistent way.

The CCA informed the audit team that several checklists are available for use by the OVs during official controls. The audit team noted that the checklists have not been up- dated since 2014 and they are not usually used by the OVs during their controls. The au- dit team assessed one checklist for official controls in poultry slaughterhouses and noted that it mainly reported the requirements laid down in Regulations (EC) Nos 853/2004 and 854/2004 and did not provide technical assistance to the OVs. 5.2.4 Training

In the slaughterhouses visited, the OVs were aware of the requirement to carry out ani- mal welfare checks and to take suitable action when needed. Animal welfare checks were also included in the planned thematic controls (see also paragraph 43) with a mini- mum frequency of two controls per year. The CCA had not issued any instructions to as- sist the OVs on the performance of these duties.

The audit team observed that different systems/methods applied during the PMI in the slaughterhouses for domestic ungulates visited and there are not specific instructions for official staff on how the PMI should be done. For example, the audit team noted: · Different incisions carried out in the different slaughterhouses by the OVs during the PMI. The OVs interviewed provided different information as regards the com- pulsory incisions and checks (visual checks, palpations) of carcases required by EU legislation. · In one of the two bovine slaughterhouses the incisions of the masseters were not 9 made in parallel to the mandible and there was one incision instead of the two re- quired by EU legislation in the outer masseters. · Some organs (i.e., stomachs and intestines) were not always subject to PMI as they were discarded immediately after evisceration. · In the porcine slaughterhouse, there was no correlation of carcases and offal (kid- neys, spleen, stomachs and intestines) during the PMI, · In certain cases, the PMI was limited to visual inspection of organs and no palpa- tion was carried out.

In all but one of the establishments visited the cleanliness of live animals before slaugh- ter was not taken into consideration in the HACCP plans. This was monitored in one of the establishments even though that procedure was not included in the HACCP plan, which also did not include clear instructions or corrective actions. This establishment was approved in 2022 and, in this regard, no observations were noted by the CA.

According to the information provided by the CA, and in addition to the RFSD audits, the FBOs own-checks are evaluated during the OV's thematic inspections. The audit and inspection reports the CA shared with the audit team did not include any remark con- cerning the above-mentioned aspects. The BFSA explained that there are no guidelines concerning assessment of HACCP systems available for the regional inspectors or the OVs. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Article 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Findings

All the FBOs at the establishments visited had a microbiological sampling plan in place. This plan is verified by the OVs during their thematic controls. There are no official in- structions in place to assist the OVs on this verification and on the subsequent official actions needed in case of non-compliance.

An official control plan, based on risk, is implemented by the CA. However, the limited 14 detection and/or recording of non-compliances at establishment level and, consequently, the lack of enforcement actions to correct the non-compliant situations compromise the effectiveness of the control system in place. In this regard, significant shortcomings in relation to the sanitary conditions and to the animal welfare conditions were noted that had not been previously identified or recorded in any level of official control.

Certain official controls at slaughterhouse level are not carried out in line with the EU requirements. In particular, the serious deviations from the legally required practical ar- rangements concerning PMI and the controls on HACCP-based procedures undermine the reliability of the OVs' decision on the fitness of meat for human consumption.

The AMI and the controls on FCI, animal identification and traceability are in general in line with the EU requirements. However, the lack of procedures for suitable recording and communication of AMI and PMI results by the OVs has, as a consequence, that no feedback is provided to the competent authorities and operators at primary production level in order to take appropriate actions when these inspections reveal a disease or con- dition that might affect human or animal health or animal welfare.

responses.response: Bulgarian Food Safety Agency established a working group 02.12.2024 representatives of the Central Competent Authority and the Food Safety Directorates. This working group carried out the task of developing a draft l for the performance of official controls in slaughterhouses for the production of meat of domestic ungulates and poultry. recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that the staff performing official controls in slaughterhouses are kept up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary as required by Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted during the on-the-spot visits that the officials did not have a suffi- cient level of knowledge of specific legal requirements to perform their duties properly, in particular concerning PMI, hazard analysis and critical control point (HACCP) sys- tems and the protection of animals at the time of killing (see also paragraphs 33, 36, 38, 48, 49 and 50). 5.2.5 Supervision and audits

A training system is in place however the findings of this audit indicate that this training is not effective or sufficient to ensure adequate knowledge of official inspectors respon- sible for the official controls in slaughterhouses.

recommendations.text: The CA should: - ensure that procedures and/or arrangements are in place to verify the effectiveness, quality and consistency of official controls as required by Article 5(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and, in particular, that official controls in slaughterhouses are carried out effectively and appropriately and - take appropriate measures to remedy the shortcomings identified through internal audits, in accordance with Article 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The official control system is supported by national legislation covering the relevant as- pects within the scope of the audit. However, the absence of guidance docu- ments/instructions for the official staff compromises the guarantees that official controls are effective and are carried out in a uniform and consistent way.

The audit reports were communicated to the RFSD concerned, which should develop an action plan with the corrective actions to be implemented for addressing the issues iden- tified. The executive director of BFSA is responsible for the enforcement of these ac- tions. The CAs explained that further follow up visits in the RFSDs where problems were noted were also planned. At the time of this audit the visits had not taken place yet. The CAs also stated that the conclusions from the audits carried out were also communi- cated to the rest of the RFSDs in order to draw their attention to the systemic issues iden- 5 tified. However, the audit team noted in the four regions visited, that were not audited by the BFSA, non-compliances similar to the ones described in paragraph 17. 5.2.6 Enforcement

Mechanisms are in place to provide guarantees about the effectiveness of the official controls. However, these mechanisms are not working properly because the supervision system over the OVs' performance is not able to uncover the weaknesses in the official controls and, when shortcomings are identified during the internal audits, these remain unsolved.

In all the slaughterhouses (for domestic ungulates) visited, the porcine animals were rou- tinely washed with pressurized water before the entrance to the slaughter line. This was also the case for bovines if they were very dirty. In one establishment it was noted that the bovines were slaughtered and de-hided while they were still wet posing an increased risk of contamination of the carcass. These practices were neither detailed in the FBO's self-control systems nor questioned by the OVs. The audit team noted that none of the FBOs implemented any written procedures in order to ensure that live animals are clean and to deal with excessively soiled animals. Moreover, the OVs met did not verify the FBOs' obligation in this regard during the AMI. This is not in line with Article 11(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The audit team observed some non-compliances in relation to the animal welfare in the slaughterhouses for ungulates visited that had not been previously noted/recorded, nei- ther by the OVs nor by the RFSDs during their visits. In all the slaughterhouses visited the maximum number of animals allowed in each of the pens in the lairage was not clear- ly indicated, contrary to what point 2.3 of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 requires. In one establishment the floor in the lairage was particularly damaged and could lead to the severe injury of the ungulates. In addition, the areas for the isolation and clinical inspection of suspected animals were not indicated or not existed. 8

Serious deficiencies were noted during the stunning and killing of birds in the poultry slaughterhouse visited. The audit team noted that a high percentage of animals showed signs of consciousness after the stunning process (e.g. birds lifting their heads, showing extensive flapping of wings, having their eyes open) and this is contrary to the require- ments of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. The audit team requested the examination of a stunned bird from the line and observed clear signs of consciousness of the animal (opening and closing of its mouth, shaking its head, reacting to touching). Neither the FBO nor the CA recognised these signs as improper stunning. In their opin- ion, those signs were part of the normal behaviour of stunned birds. In addition, the audit team noted that most of the birds suffered pre-stunning electrical shocks when entering the water bath, as the wings and the body of the birds were touching the water of the stunner before their heads, and there was no `breast comforter' available. All these ob- servations are contrary to requirements provided in Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. No corrective actions were requested (i.e. stopping the line) by the CAs in this slaughter- house during these findings. Post-mortem inspection

At the slaughterhouses for ungulates visited, the practical arrangements for PMI were not fully in line with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/627: there was not a clear PMI point, with adequate working conditions and with the necessary equipment (ade- quate lighting, equipment for the recording of the PMI results, equipment for the disin- fection of the OV's knives, dedicated wash-hand basins), designated. As a consequence, the OV could not easily perform a visual examination of all the external surfaces and of the cavities of bovine carcases. Moreover, as the OV was carrying out the PMI checks in different locations in the slaughter line, it was not clear the point in the slaughter line where the carcases are declared fit for human consumption (e.g. before or after the wash- ing by the FBO). In one of the establishments the OV had to move to a separate room for the examination of the heads of bovine carcases, as this was the location decided by the FBO, making difficult the correlation between carcases and heads.

The audit team observed that different systems/methods applied during the PMI in the slaughterhouses for domestic ungulates visited and there are not specific instructions for official staff on how the PMI should be done. For example, the audit team noted: · Different incisions carried out in the different slaughterhouses by the OVs during the PMI. The OVs interviewed provided different information as regards the com- pulsory incisions and checks (visual checks, palpations) of carcases required by EU legislation. · In one of the two bovine slaughterhouses the incisions of the masseters were not 9 made in parallel to the mandible and there was one incision instead of the two re- quired by EU legislation in the outer masseters. · Some organs (i.e., stomachs and intestines) were not always subject to PMI as they were discarded immediately after evisceration. · In the porcine slaughterhouse, there was no correlation of carcases and offal (kid- neys, spleen, stomachs and intestines) during the PMI, · In certain cases, the PMI was limited to visual inspection of organs and no palpa- tion was carried out.

Serious deviations from the requirements of the EU legislation on PMI were noted by the audit team in the poultry slaughterhouse visited. More in particular: · The PMI was carried out by the OVs (with the support of slaughterhouse staff). There was no designated and suitably equipped area for the PMI (lack of equip- ment for the recording of the results and the disinfection of the knives, no mirror for the inspection of all the external surfaces, no additional lighting, etc.). · There was no PMI of the offal. The offal was collected and transferred to a sepa- rate part of the establishment to be washed. There was no correlation between car- cases and offal. The livers and intestines of the birds were discarded immediately after evisceration. · There was no recording of the PMI results (neither by the slaughterhouse staff nor by the OV). No relevant information on the cause and the exact quantities of the meat condemned was recorded in the PMI logbook. · After the PMI, the carcases (or part of them), declared unfit for human consump- tion, were collected by the slaughterhouse staff to be disposed. The OV (or the OA) did not carry out (or did not record) any inspection of a sample of these car- cases (or parts of them), contrary to Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In addition, there was no daily inspection of the viscera and body cavities of a repre- 10 sentative sample of each flock by the OV (or an OA) as also required by the same Article. 5.3.2 Official controls over food business operators' obligations Food Chain Information (FCI) and animal identification Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in conjunction with its Annex II Section III and Article 9 and 10, 40, 41 42 and 43.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

An official control plan, based on risk, is implemented by the CA. However, the limited 14 detection and/or recording of non-compliances at establishment level and, consequently, the lack of enforcement actions to correct the non-compliant situations compromise the effectiveness of the control system in place. In this regard, significant shortcomings in relation to the sanitary conditions and to the animal welfare conditions were noted that had not been previously identified or recorded in any level of official control.

Certain official controls at slaughterhouse level are not carried out in line with the EU requirements. In particular, the serious deviations from the legally required practical ar- rangements concerning PMI and the controls on HACCP-based procedures undermine the reliability of the OVs' decision on the fitness of meat for human consumption.

recommendations.text: To review the application of enforcement measures in order to guarantee that where non-compliances are established, appropriate measures are taken to ensure that the operator concerned remedies the non-compliance and prevents further occurrences of such non-compliance, as required by Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In some of the establishments visited, the audit team identified a significant number of longstanding non-compliances that had not been previously identified or recorded neither by the OVs during their daily presence nor by the RFSD during their inspections (see paragraph 15) and therefore no enforcement measures had been applied to resolve them. In particular, in one slaughterhouse that the audit team selected, serious non-compliances as regards the sanitary and maintenance conditions were observed. The OVs and the RFSD inspectors responsible for the controls at this establishment explained that they had also detected some of these problems in the past. However, they did not record them in the reports. The OVs added that, in some cases, they had verbally requested the FBO to repair certain parts of the establishment (e.g. the lairage). Despite that, the FBO took no action to resolve the non-compliances observed, the OVs did not impose subsequent enforcement actions and, as a result, the situation remained unchanged.

In the same establishment above-mentioned, the FBO refused to facilitate access to the audit team and CAs to three locked chilling rooms, two of them directly connected to the slaughter area. The OVs that were permanently present in the establishment for the last 4 months had no access to these parts of the premises. The OVs did not consider this situa- tion could be an issue as the FBO told them that these chilling rooms did not belong to the approved part of the establishment and, therefore, had been locked. The CA managed to get access to one of the chilling rooms, breaking the lock, in the presence of the audit team. This was a cold store where large quantities of frozen meat/meat products (aprox. 10 tonnes) were stored in a way which rendered the meat and products unfit for human consumption. The other two chilling rooms were opened when the audit team was not present (i.e. during lunch time). When the team came back to the slaughterhouse, got ac- cess to the rooms and found that one was empty and, the other one was filled with transport cages. In relation to that establishment, and subsequent to the audit team visit, the CA committed to applying enforcement actions. Evidence of the actions taken were provided to the audit team before the end of the audit (condemnation of the meat in ques- tion and temporary suspension of this establishment's activities). 6 Conclusions on competent authorities

The system in place provides official staff with the authority to enforce legal require- ments. However, the effectiveness of this system is compromised because the official controls are not able to detect non-compliances, or they do not record them and so, en- forcement actions are not imposed. Moreover, when non compliances are detected, offi- cials do not always impose enforcement actions to solve the issues.

All these ob- servations are contrary to requirements provided in Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. No corrective actions were requested (i.e. stopping the line) by the CAs in this slaughter- house during these findings. Post-mortem inspection

In addition to the thematic controls and the AMI and PMI, the OVs are also tasked with the daily monitoring of the hygiene conditions during slaughtering operations, imposing enforcement measures when necessary. The audit team received some written examples of notices (prescriptions) issued by the OVs as evidence of such enforcement actions in the establishments visited. It was noted that they referred to the cleaning of the premises or the hygiene practices and not to the long-standing deficiencies described above. Findings

In all but one of the establishments visited, the premises, facilities and hygiene practices were in general satisfactory. However, some deficiencies were noted by the audit team that had not previously been observed/recorded by the CAs (e.g. cleaning of the floor with high pressure splashing water, while exposed carcasses were present, with risk of contamination of meat, dirty overhead rails above exposed meat, lack of cleaning and disinfection of footwear of the workers entering the facilities).

Serious non-compliances were noted in one slaughterhouse of domestic ungulates which had not been detected and/or recorded previously by any level of official controls, nei- ther by the OV not the RFSD (see also paragraphs 20 and 21). More specifically the au- dit team noted: damage to the floors, walls and the ceiling in the evisceration and areas for further processing of the carcases, rusty equipment above exposed meat, damaged equipment in several parts of the establishment, broken surfaces, dirty chillers with sur- faces not able to be suitably cleaned and/ or disinfected, gaps between the floors and the external doors, not allowing suitable pest control, and bad hygiene standards in several parts on the establishment that were linked to the slaughterhouse and were approved for cutting and preparation of meat.

In the establishments visited, the FBOs considered the chilling temperatures of meat as the most important points to control. In all but one of the establishments the evisceration (and the risk of faecal contamination) was not considered as a control point in the HACCP systems assessed. In all the establishments visited, the corrective action provid- ed for in the HACCP plans in case of faecal contamination of carcases was the cleaning with water.

In all but one of the establishments visited the cleanliness of live animals before slaugh- ter was not taken into consideration in the HACCP plans. This was monitored in one of the establishments even though that procedure was not included in the HACCP plan, which also did not include clear instructions or corrective actions. This establishment was approved in 2022 and, in this regard, no observations were noted by the CA.

The audit team noted that in two of the domestic ungulate slaughterhouses visited the OVs had detected (during the last inspections carried out in 2024) that the frequency of the microbiological sampling for process hygiene criteria on meat was not in line with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. In response, action plans were provided by the FBOs to 13 correct this non-compliance. In one of these cases the OV accepted a fortnightly (and not weekly) frequency for the sampling of carcases for Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and aerobic colony count despite the fact that no negative results in thirty (or six) consecu- tive weeks had been obtained previously. Moreover, the deadline for the FBO to comply with this obligation was 7 months. To be also noted that in the HACCP plan of this es- tablishment, approved in 2022, the relevant sampling frequency was one sample per month and that was accepted by the CA during the approval procedure.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official veterinarians record and evaluate the results of ante- mortem and post-mortem inspection and, where the inspection reveals the presence of any disease or condition that might affect human or animal health, or compromise animal welfare, communicates this information in accordance with Article 39 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: None of the OVs in the slaughterhouses visited recorded the outcome of the AMI on-the- spot. Therefore, information about the animals that passed satisfactorily the AMI is not transferred to the slaughterhouse (no system of positive release existed). This system does not provide guarantees that only those animals that had been subject to AMI and had been declared fit for slaughter could be processed by the FBO. The CA explained that this is the common practice in smaller slaughterhouses as there is direct communica- tion between the OVs carrying out AMI and the OVs in the PMI positions. The audit team noted that the CA has not issued any instruction/procedure requiring OVs perform- ing AMI to keep records of the outcome (e.g. record all the relevant findings of AMI) and pass this information to the slaughterhouse operator before accepting the animals for slaughter.

At the slaughterhouses visited it was observed that in the logbooks, that are filled out once the slaughter has taken place, the information concerning the identification of the animals and the final AMI decision were recorded (fit for slaughter or not). No further details in relation to animal health or welfare were indicated.

In the same slaughterhouses the OVs did not have an adequate system to record PMI de- tails. In all the cases observed the total quantities of condemnations were recorded in the PMI logbook. However, the specific reasons for which a carcase/meat have been con- demned and the link to a particular batch of animals was not reported (e.g. it was docu- mented the total weight of offal rejected due to pneumonia or ascites without describing the exact offal). Therefore, the system in place does not allow the FBOs and OVs to pro- vide feedback on information that could affect human or animal health, or compromise animal welfare, to other interested parties (e.g. FBO responsible for the holding of prov- enance, CAs responsible for supervising these holding). The CA explained that currently there is no instruction or template model on how and when the communication with the holding of provenance should take place.

More in particular: · The PMI was carried out by the OVs (with the support of slaughterhouse staff). The offal was collected and transferred to a sepa- rate part of the establishment to be washed. There was no correlation between car- cases and offal. The livers and intestines of the birds were discarded immediately after evisceration. · There was no recording of the PMI results (neither by the slaughterhouse staff nor by the OV). No relevant information on the cause and the exact quantities of the meat condemned was recorded in the PMI logbook. · After the PMI, the carcases (or part of them), declared unfit for human consump- tion, were collected by the slaughterhouse staff to be disposed. The OV (or the OA) did not carry out (or did not record) any inspection of a sample of these car- cases (or parts of them), contrary to Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In addition, there was no daily inspection of the viscera and body cavities of a repre- 10 sentative sample of each flock by the OV (or an OA) as also required by the same Article. 5.3.2 Official controls over food business operators' obligations Food Chain Information (FCI) and animal identification Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in conjunction with its Annex II Section III and Article 9 and 10, 40, 41 42 and 43.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

The AMI and the controls on FCI, animal identification and traceability are in general in line with the EU requirements. However, the lack of procedures for suitable recording and communication of AMI and PMI results by the OVs has, as a consequence, that no feedback is provided to the competent authorities and operators at primary production level in order to take appropriate actions when these inspections reveal a disease or con- dition that might affect human or animal health or animal welfare.

audits.title: evaluate controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that decisions on non-compliance for pharmacologically active substances are based on assessment of the analytical value of the testing against the decision limit for confirmation (CC). Relevant EU legislation: Article 5(1) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: The audit team noted that in all of the six non-compliant results for pharmacologically active substances, the establishing of the non-compliance was not based on pertinent legal requirements 51 since the results obtained had not been assessed against the decision limit for confirmation (CC) as per the laboratory reports seen by the audit team (neither other documents observed had any reference to CC). Furthermore, in three cases of the six results for pharmacologically active substances, the official decision on non-compliance had been made based solely on the outcome of screening testing only without further analysing with a confirmatory method, which is contrary to EU legislation 52. Conclusions on follow-up and enforcement

While the actions taken on non-compliant results were rapid, comprehensive and effective, the decision making on the non-compliance status of the test results for pharmacologically active substances was not based on applicable legal requirements which puts in question the legal validity of the non-compliance decisions made and consequent actions taken by the competent authority. 47 Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 48 Articles 4, 5 and 6 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. 49 Articles 5(1)(2) and 6(3)(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. 50 As defined in Article 1(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1644. 51 Article 5(1) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 52 Part 1.1.2. of Chapter I of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 12 5.6. Laboratories, methods of analysis, method validation and internal quality control

recommendations.text: To ensure that (i) the validation of analytical methods incorporates all mandatory performance characteristics, (ii) the values obtained are assessed against established legal criteria, in particular for trueness (by recovery) and precision (under within-laboratory reproducibility conditions), and (iii) impact of deviations from said criteria on the outcome of the validation is analysed in a documented traceable manner. Relevant EU legislation: Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808.

citations.text: With regard to method validation, the audit team noted the following: a) The majority of analytical methods had been validated in accordance with the applicable EU legal framework that was in force at the time of validation 57. Revalidation of these methods in line with the requirements of the EU legislation in force 58 was ongoing at the time of the audit. b) The methods were validated at the level of interest 59. c) Across all validation files scrutinised, the audit team observed a number of trueness (by recovery) and precision (under within-laboratory reproducibility conditions) values which did not meet the performance criteria established by EU legislation 60. The potential impact of those deviations on the outcome of the validation was not analysed by the laboratory in a documented traceable manner 61. d) In general, the assessment of method ruggedness was not performed and assessed by the laboratory, and stability studies of the analytes in both solution and matrix were not conducted, which is a mandatory performance characteristic to be determined during validation 62. In relation to stability, the laboratory referred to scientific literature or information from another laboratory. Nevertheless, none of the sources presented unambiguously demonstrated that identical conditions had been applied (e.g., storage temperature and duration); this approach is not in line with pertinent EU requirements 63. e) The validation data for the ELISA-based screening method for antimicrobial substances included comprehensive evidence demonstrating that the validation had been conducted in accordance with applicable EU requirements 60. In contrast, the validation documentation for the microbiological screening tests of antibiotics lacked essential information on the experimental design, including details on the number and type of replicate analyses used to determine the detection capability for screening (CC). This omission prevented proper assessment of the method's reliability and compliance with EU validation requirements 64. 57 Commission Decision 2002/657/EC. 58 Chapter 2 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 59 Article 2(19) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 60 Parts 1.2.2.1. and 1.2.2.2. of Chapter 1 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 61 Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 62 Part 2.1. of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 63 Footnote (#) to Table 5 in part 2.1. of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 64 Part 2.7 of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 14 f) In quinolones and dyes methods, only four fortification levels with four replicates were applied; this approach differs from the requirements of pertinent EU legislation 65.

Notwithstanding that all of the laboratories comprising the laboratory network are adequately designated, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025, have all of the methods in the laboratories' scope of accreditation and operate sufficient internal quality control, deficiencies in the method validation and the lack of confirmation of the results obtained through screening methods undermine the confidence that the competent authority can have in the reliability of the results generated by the laboratory network. 65 Part 2.2.1.4. of Chapter 2 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 66 Chapter 3 of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 67 Part 1.1.2. of Chapter I of Annex I to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 68 Article 38(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 69 Point 7 of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 15 6. OVERALL CONCLUSION Notwithstanding that the implementation of official controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products is largely in line with EU legal requirements and planned arrangements, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by (i) deficiencies in decision-making in case of identified non-compliances, and (ii) shortcomings in method validation. If left unaddressed, these have the potential to cumulatively reduce the effectiveness of residue controls and consequently undermine confidence in official guarantees on the chemical safety of food. 7. CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 13 June 2025 with representatives of the BFSA, including its regional branches, and the BFSA laboratory. At this meeting, the audit team presented its main preliminary findings and conclusions. The BFSA representatives did not express disagreement and undertook to take the actions necessary to address the shortcomings identified. 8. RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authority is requested to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. With regard to those shortcomings noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authority is, nevertheless, requested to address these. The effectiveness of the actions taken to address such shortcomings will be assessed in future audits on this topic. audits.title: follow-up audit on the official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union through the border control post Kapitan Andreevo and its compliance with Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that the border control post Kapitan Andreevo complies with the rules on minimum requirements for border control posts for the categories of animals and goods for which it has been designated, in particular with respect to the hygiene and maintenance of the unloading and housing areas for animals, categories ungulates and equidae, and the overall capacity of the premises are appropriate to the nature and volume of the categories of goods of non-animal origin, plants, plant products and other objects subject to official controls at the BCP.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 64(3)(b), (h) and (i) of the OCR and Articles 3(3) and 5(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

citations.text: The audit team noted however that: · Despite the measures taken, birds were still present and nesting in the roof covering the unloading and housing areas for ungulates and equidae, which were consequently not kept clean nor free of pests, and in that respect did not therefore ensure the proper handling of animals to avoid cross contamination nor compliance with relevant biosecurity standards in order to prevent the spread of diseases, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) and (i) of the OCR. · The sharp edges, rust and flaking paint noted by the previous audit, were still evident in the unloading and housing areas, which were not maintained so as to avoid injury of the animals and ensure their safety, which is not in line with Article 5(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 and are not easy to clean, which is not in line with Articles 3(3) of same regulation. 11 The BFSA informed the audit team that the necessary funding to address the shortcomings in the animal facilities had been allocated, and the necessary remedial work is planned to start in late 2025. · Despite the measures taken by the BFSA aimed at improving the organisation and efficiency of the official controls at the BCP, the BCP facilities for plants, plant products and other objects, and to a lesser extent, for goods of non-animal origin are, as noted by the previous audit, not appropriate to the volume of these categories of goods requiring official controls at the BCP. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR. The overall capacity of the unloading areas remains limited to the contents of only one means of transport at a time. The BFSA informed the audit team that the BCP has capacity to handle up to 500 freight vehicles/day, while in peak season (i.e. winter) 1 400 to 1 500 vehicles/day may be expected. Conclusions on recommendation 2022-7637-12 of the previous audit

However, despite the many improvements at the BCP Kaptan Andreevo, the animal facilities for the categories ungulates and equidae still do not comply with the rules for minimum requirements for BCPs with respect to the hygiene and maintenance of the facilities, and the overall capacity of the premises for performing official controls on goods of non-animal origin and plants, plant products and other objects, is not appropriate to the nature and volume of the categories of goods handled, especially at peak times.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the frequency of identity and physical checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin are carried out in accordance with the detailed rules for the performance of those checks.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 8 of and Annexes I and II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793, and Article 5(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1158.

citations.text: The audit team noted, based on data provided by the BFSA, and extracted from TRACES, that the frequencies of identity and physical checks performed on consignments of goods of non-animal origin in 2024 were in general, similar to those found by the previous audit: peppers (13.2% checked vs 20% required), apricot kernel (16.7% vs 50%), cumin (7.3% vs 30%), oregano (14.3 vs 20%), dried figs (10.4% vs 20%), vine leaves (21.4% vs 50%) pistachios (15.4% vs 30%) from Türkiye, and hazelnuts from Georgia (17,5% vs 20%), which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 6 and 8 and Annexes I and II of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 and mushrooms (13.3% vs 20% required) from Türkiye, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1158. Conclusion on recommendation 2022-7637-8 of the previous audit

The corrective action taken to date by the competent authority has not been effective in ensuring that the frequency of identity and physical checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin are carried out in accordance with the detailed rules for the performance of those checks. 5.2.8. Recommendation 2022-7637-9 To ensure BCP officials (a) check with the competent authorities of the control point whether consignments of goods of non-animal origin have arrived in cases where the authorities have not received confirmation of arrival within 15 days from the day on which the transfer of a consignment to the control point was authorised, (b) inform Customs and (c) determine the actual location of said goods. 8

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on food and seeds are performed in particular on a risk basis taking account of identified risks in line with Article 9(1)(a)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The FCD has an annual risk-based sampling and analysis plan for GMOs in food. It was planned to take 89 food samples in both 2024 and 2025 for analysis for GMOs under this plan. Raw materials based on soya, rapeseed and maize, ready-to-eat foods, foods for infants and young children based on soya and/or maize and rapeseed oil are targeted for sampling and analysis. All samples are from the internal market (i.e. there are no planned samples at the point of import) and are mainly drawn from manufacturers of snack foods, bakery/confectionary products and meat-based products. Each region is allocated a defined number of samples, and FCD regional staff determine the specific products to sample (according to the instructions described in finding 6) and the sampling locations. Bulgaria grows over 12 000 ha of rice and 3 500 ha of tomatoes per year and has been involved in RASFF notifications related to genetically modified micro-organisms (GMMOs) (finding 70). There are known cases of genetic modification in foods such as rice, linseed, papaya, potato and tomato or GMMOs. The FCD did not plan to collect samples of, at least, rice, tomatoes and GMMOs in 2024 and 2025. It stated that it has never included foodstuffs other than soya, rapeseed and maize in its planned sampling and analysis programme for GMOs. This indicates that the risks associated with commodities other than soya, rapeseed and maize are not taken into account when planning official controls, which is not in line with Article 9(1)(a)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The BFSA notifies the IASAS in writing within three days of all imports of seed and propagating material. IASAS staff conduct a documentary check on these consignments in all cases. IASAS staff also conduct documentary checks on seed lots of EU and Bulgarian origin. The MANCP 2024-2026, and the annual control programme for GMOs in seeds, both specify that 10 seed samples should be tested for GMOs each year, comprising five maize samples, three rapeseed samples and two soyabean samples. Bulgarian farmers grow over 12 000 ha of rice and 3 500 ha tomatoes each year. The area devoted to soya has declined sharply from 14 000 ha in 2016 and 11 500 ha in 2017 to 500-600 ha in 2024 and 2025. Despite the risks associated with both rice and tomatoes (crops in which genetic modification is known to have occurred) and the collapse in the area devoted to soya, the IASAS stated that the annual control programme for GMOs in seeds has never been changed to include other crops and/or to change the numbers of samples to be analysed each year. Therefore, the annual control programme for GMOs in seeds does not reflect all identified risks (i.e. the risks associated with crops in which 7 genetic modification is known to have occurred other than maize, rapeseed and soya) as required by Article 9(1)(a)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Consequently, it does not meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, as some crops which are grown in Bulgaria and which may be subject to genetic modification (e.g. rice and tomatoes) have never been included in the scope of the IASIS sampling and analysis programme for GMOs in seeds. As a result of this deficiency, GM seeds of these crops would not be detected in the course of planned official controls on seeds. Conclusion on planning official controls

The planned official controls for GMOs in food and seeds provide a reasonable level of assurance that food marketed in Bulgaria and seeds sown in Bulgaria do not contain GMOs but are weakened by the failure to include controls on all foods and seeds where genetic modification is known to occur.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on feed are performed in particular with appropriate frequency set out in the planned control programme in line with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In 2024, the RFSDs completed 83% of the planned number of controls (dealing with all aspects of feed legislation, including GMOs) on feed business operators. The figures for 2025 were not finalised at the time of the audit but were broadly comparable to 2024, meaning that in both years the CAs failed to perform official controls on GMOs in feed with appropriate frequency as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. As part of these controls, inspectors were required to conduct controls on GMOs at all operators where GM labelled feeds were present. This amounted to 370 and 295 controls in 2024 and 2025 respectively. Seventeen of the 28 regions completed the planned number of controls, but five regions completed 50% or less of the planned number in both 2024 and 2025. The BFSA explained that this was due to additional work associated with exports in some regions and the limited number of staff dealing with feed in these regions. While staff can be transferred between and within regions as described in finding 2, the audit team noted that this possibility had not been used to redistribute staff to ensure that all regions were able to implement the planned number of risk-based controls.

In both 2024 and 2025, the RFSDs took 18 risk-based feed for analysis for GMOs, rather than the 28 samples in the annual plans, thereby failing to perform official controls on GMOs in feed with appropriate frequency as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The FCABPD attributed this discrepancy to the heavy workload on staff and difficulties in obtaining relevant feed samples. The 18 samples in 2024 comprised one feed additive, five compound feeds (four of which had GM ingredients declared on their labels) and twelve feed materials (two of which were declared to be GM). The 18 samples in 2025 comprised one feed additive, six compound feeds (five of which had GM ingredients 10 declared on their labels) and eleven feed materials (one of which was declared to be GM). The 23 feed materials sampled and analysed over the two years were all derived from maize, soya or rapeseed.

Official controls provide a reasonable level of assurance that food and feed marketed in Bulgaria, including rice and rice products imported from China, comply with EU requirements regarding GMOs. Official controls on feed are weakened as just 66% of the planned sampling and analysis programme is completed. Official controls on food are weakened by the failure to include all foods where genetic modification is known to occur in the sampling and analysis programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that: - the designations of laboratories include a detailed description of the tasks (i.e. the scope of analysis for GMOs) to be carried out as required by Article 37(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. - designated laboratories analyse official samples using methodologies capable of detecting all known GM events in seeds of relevant crops so that seeds sown in Bulgaria are free of GMOs, thereby complying with Directive 2001/18/EC), as required by Article 4(5) of that Directive. - designated laboratories analyse official samples using methodologies capable of detecting all known GM events in relevant foods and feeds to ensure that feed and food subject to official controls do not contain non-authorised GM events, or GMOs above the legally permitted threshold, in cases where it is not labelled as containing, consisting or produced from GMOs as required by Articles 4(2), 12, 13, 16(2), 24 and 25 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003.

citations.text: The audit team examined analysis reports for three seed samples of maize, soya and rapeseed from July 2025. The analysis report for maize showed that 21 (48%) of the 44 known genetic modification events in maize listed by the EURL GMFF were analysed. The analysis report for soya showed that 14 (48%) of the 29 known genetic modification events in soya were analysed. The report for rapeseed showed that the sample was analysed using screening analysis for P35S and T-nos. Based on information provided by the EURL GMFF, this screening analysis is capable of detecting 11 (65%) of the 17 known genetic modification events in rapeseed. The NCPHA confirmed that these analysis reports are representative of the scope of analysis conducted on all seed samples in 2024 and 2025. The limited range of analysis performed for genetic modification events in seeds (48% of known genetic modification events in maize and soya and 65% of known genetic modification events in rapeseed) means that the measures taken by the CAs under Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC are not sufficient to ensure that seeds sown in Bulgaria are free of GMOs, and therefore that they comply with the requirements of Directive 2001/18/EC.

The NCPHA also confirmed that food samples are also tested using the same approach, and therefore the same proportion of maize, soya and rapeseed genetic modification events are detected in food. This range of analysis is not sufficient to ensure that food marketed in Bulgaria does not contain non-authorised genetic modification events, or GMOs above the legally permitted threshold in cases where it is not labelled as containing, consisting or produced from GMOs, as required by Articles 4(2), 12, and 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003.

The audit team examined analysis reports for four official feed samples from July, October, November and December 2025. The four samples were all screened for P35S, P- FMV and T-nos. The FCABPD confirmed that this is standard practice for all feed samples, and added that if the screening had indicated GM material was present, further analysis would have been completed. In the four cass examined, the screening analysis showed negative results, so no further analysis was completed. Based on the information provided by the EURL GMFF, this screening analysis is capable of detecting 30 (68%) of 44 genetic modification events in maize, 15 (52%) of 29 genetic modification events in soya and 13 (76%) of 17 genetic modification events in rapeseed. This range of analysis is not sufficient to ensure that feed marketed in Bulgaria does not contain non-authorised genetic modification events, or GMOs above the legally permitted threshold in cases where it is not labelled as containing, consisting or produced from GMOs, as required by Articles 16(2), 24 and 25 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. 15

The FCD and the IASAS both stated that they designated the NCPHA to conduct analysis for GMOs on the basis that the laboratory is accredited for this work as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The designations do not include a detailed description of the tasks (i.e. the scope of analysis for GMOs) to be carried out as required by Article 37(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Similarly, the agreement between the FCABPD and the private laboratory does not include a detailed description of the tasks (i.e. the scope of analysis for GMOs) to be carried out). As a consequence of this deficiency, the laboratories analyse samples using a limited analytical scope capable of detecting 50% of known genetic modification events in maize, soya and rapeseed in food and seeds and two thirds of known genetic modification events in maize, soya and rapeseed in feed as described in findings 57, 58 and 60. The NCPHA stated that it can test for a wider range of genetic modification events than currently conducted on food and seed samples if specifically required by the FCD or the IASAS. The audit team noted that the scope of accreditation of the private laboratory used by the FCABPD covers a wide range of screening methods, and a wide range of specific events in soya, maize, rapeseed and cotton, in addition to events in rice, sugar beet and potatoes, meaning that it could also analyse for a much wider range of genetic modification events if specifically requested to do this by the FCABPD.

Official controls on seeds provide a reasonable level of assurance that conventional seeds of the most widely grown crops do not contain GMOs. The level of assurance provided by controls is weakened by the failure to include all seeds where genetic modification is known to occur in the control programme.

Official controls provide a reasonable level of assurance that food and feed marketed in Bulgaria, including rice and rice products imported from China, comply with EU requirements regarding GMOs. Official controls on feed are weakened as just 66% of the planned sampling and analysis programme is completed. Official controls on food are weakened by the failure to include all foods where genetic modification is known to occur in the sampling and analysis programme.

The failure to specify the range of analysis for GMOs to performed on official samples, and the limited range of analysis performed as a result, means that some non-authorised genetic modification events (in seeds, food and feed), and some cases of GMOs above the legally permitted threshold (in food and feed), are not consistently detected during official controls. 16
